sens: To look attentively at something or someone
To observe intentionally what is happening
To see and understand the meaning of what one sees
To be seen, to be looked at by others
G2300.detail: 1. The verb primarily denotes the act of fixing one's gaze on something or someone with attention and intention. It is a deliberate look, not a mere passing glance: when Jesus sees Levi the tax collector sitting at the tax booth (Luke 5:27), he truly looks at him, not by chance. 2. The word can also express the observation of a situation, a spectacle that one sees unfolding. Jesus tells his disciples to lift their eyes and look at the fields that are white for harvest (John 4:35): it is about seeing and seizing the present moment. 3. When one contemplates, one does not just see with the eyes: one understands, one grasps the meaning. The disciples contemplated the glory of the Word made flesh (John 1:14), which means they perceived his divine majesty. The Jews who saw what Jesus did in raising Lazarus believed in him (John 11:45). 4. The verb can finally mean 'to be seen' or 'to be looked at': the Pharisees do all their deeds to be seen by men (Matthew 23:5).
G2300.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of contemplating with admiration or astonishment, like when one watches a captivating spectacle. In classical Greek, this verb often carries a nuance of admiring contemplation. The New Testament has retained the literal meaning of 'to look attentively', but without necessarily implying astonishment.
G2300.emploi: This verb appears 23 times in the New Testament, mainly in John (7 occurrences), Luke, and Matthew. It is always used in the literal and physical sense: looking at a person (Jesus sees Levi, Matthew 22:11), observing a scene (John 4:35, the disciples watch the ascension in Acts 1:11), contemplating Jesus himself (John 1:14: 'we have contemplated his glory'). Sometimes the verb has a moral shade: being seen or observed by others, particularly for the works one does (Matthew 6:1, Matthew 23:5). In 1 John 1:1 and 4:12, it is about seeing God or Christ with one's own eyes: an act that establishes faith.
G2300.portee: This verb reminds us that seeing is never passive: to truly look is to give attention and understanding to what one sees. For the disciple, contemplating Jesus is much more than just crossing paths with him visually: it is to seek the glory of the Son of God. And for our lives, the word warns us that we ourselves are being looked at, seen by God and by others: this calls for authenticity.

sens: To be delivered to the gaze of a crowd for one's shame or misfortune
To be made public and an object of contempt or derision
G2301.detail: 1. The word paints the image of a person staged before all, like in a theater, to be seen and judged: it is to be 'exposed in spectacle', according to the expression of the Psalter. In Hebrews 10:33, persecuted Christians are described as 'exposed as in spectacle to reproaches' — they are seen by all, publicly humiliated, subjected to mockery and suffering. 2. More broadly, it means to be made visible intentionally, either for shame or for contempt: the word implies a public exposure that causes dishonor or pain. This public exposure amplifies the humiliation: it is not suffering alone, it is suffering under the eyes of all.
G2301.origine: The word comes from the Greek θέατρον (theatron), the place where one looks and is looked at. The prefix θεα- denotes the spectacle, what is seen. The verb literally means 'to make a spectacle of', to transform someone into a spectacle. It is a rare word in ancient Greek, mostly used in contexts of humiliation or public exposure.
G2301.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 10:33, in an exhortation to Christians enduring persecution. The author encourages them by reminding them that they are not alone: others have also experienced this public exposure to insults and torments. It is a powerful verb to describe not only physical suffering but also the social humiliation that early Christians endured.
G2301.portee: This word reminds believers who suffer persecution that their trial is not secret or anonymous — it unfolds under the eyes of all. But the context of Hebrews 10:33 shows that this public exposure does not negate solidarity: others have endured the same thing, and believers are never truly alone. It is a call to perseverance in the face of shame.

sens: Building or place intended for gatherings and public spectacles
The audience watching a spectacle
A performance or representation given in public
What is exposed to view, staged to be seen
G2302.detail: 1. The theater is primarily a building, an amphitheater where crowds gather to attend performances. In Ephesus, during the riot provoked by Paul's preaching, the crowd rushes 'to the theater' (Acts 19:29), which is the quintessential public place where people gather en masse — it is a place of assembly and tumult. 2. The theater also refers to the entire audience present: it is all those who are watching, who are there to see. It is the whole public, considered as a unit. 3. The word can mean the spectacle itself, what is shown, presented before a crowd. It is the public event that attracts attention. 4. Metaphorically, it is what is exposed, staged before the eyes of the world. Paul writes that God has made the apostles 'a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men' (1 Corinthians 4:9): their entire life is observed, judged, contemplated as a tragic representation where everyone sees their distress and suffering.
G2302.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb 'to see' (θεάομαι, theaomai). A theater is literally the place where one looks, where those who observe gather. The root expresses the idea of spectacle, vision, of something delivered to public view. This word was natural in Greek to designate both the building and what happens there.
G2302.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. Twice in the account of Ephesus (Acts 19:29, 31): the theater is the actual building where artisans and the crowd rush to protest against Paul and his disciples. It is a space of tumult and danger, where the whole city can gather in urgency. A third time in 1 Corinthians 4:9, Paul uses it figuratively: the apostles have become a 'spectacle', meaning that their miserable situation is exposed, visible to all — to the whole world, to angels and to men. The meaning shifts from the physical building to the image of public exposure.
G2302.portee: This word reminds the reader that the life of the Christian — particularly that of the apostle — unfolds under the gaze of all. There is nothing hidden: our sufferings, our difficulties, our faithfulness are seen by the world, by angels, by God himself. It is both a call to authenticity and an invitation to understand that our existence has a cosmic significance, that it bears witness before a vast assembly. The biblical theater is not a place of entertainment: it is where truth is revealed.

sens: yellow flammable substance that burns with a pungent odor
sulfur rain or fire sent from heaven as divine punishment
eternal torment associated with fire in the afterlife
G2303.detail:
1. Sulfur is a yellow material that ignites easily and emits a foul smoke — a substance well-known in antiquity. Luke 17:29 describes a "rain of fire and sulfur" falling on Sodom, an image of judgment by fire from heaven.

2. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew term for this mineral. The Bible associates it from the account of Sodom with the fearsome action of God: sulfur is not an ordinary substance; it is the instrument of miraculous punishment.

3. In Revelation, sulfur becomes a symbol of eternal torment. Revelation 19:20 and 20:10 speak of a "lake of fire and sulfur" where the beast, the false prophet, and the devil will be thrown. This sulfurous fire never goes out: it represents God's final judgment against evil.
G2303.origine: The Greek word theion literally means "that which belongs to the gods" or "of divine nature," because the ancients saw in the sulfur that erupts from the earth a wonderful and supernatural substance. In biblical Hebrew, it was called "gofrit" (גׇּפְרִית), from a root meaning "to burn." Sulfur was a rare and feared mineral, naturally associated with manifestations of divine judgment.
G2303.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, primarily in Revelation. Luke 17:29 is the only occurrence outside of Revelation: it recounts the historical judgment of Sodom. Then, Revelation uses sulfur to describe the final punishment: first in Revelation 9:17-18, where sulfur coming from the mouths of the apocalyptic horses kills a third of humanity, and then regularly in Revelation 14:10, 19:20, 20:10, and 21:8 to designate the eternal lake of fire. The word thus shifts from the concrete (the substance) to the figurative (the symbol of judgment).
G2303.portee: Sulfur reminds the reader that God judges evil with formidable and visible force. For the Christian, this word warns of the reality of divine judgment and its eternal consequences. But it also invites reflection on the grace received in Christ: we are saved from this lake of fire by the sacrifice of the Lamb.

sens: Belonging to God, coming from God
Having the characteristics of God, His nature or power
The divinity itself, the divine essence
G2304.detail:
1. The word "divine" qualifies what belongs to God or emanates from Him: it is the adjective derived from the noun God (theós). In 2 Peter 1:3, Paul speaks of God's "divine power" — this power that comes from God and belongs only to Him.
2. In a deeper sense, "divine" designates what shares the very nature of God. In 2 Peter 1:4, believers are called to become "partakers of the divine nature" by fleeing from lust: they are invited to reflect God's characteristics in their lives.
3. The word can also refer to divinity itself, the divine essence as a reality. In Acts 17:29, Paul rejects the idea that "divinity" can be represented by gold or silver idols: true divinity transcends any material image.
G2304.origine: The word comes from the Greek name for "God" (theós) with the suffix -ios that makes it an adjective. It is an essentially Greek word: the Hebrew Old Testament did not have an exact equivalent, but Greek translators used it to render expressions concerning God, His power, and His nature (as in Exodus 31:3 where the Spirit of God gives divine wisdom to the craftsman Bezalel).
G2304.emploi: The word appears only 3 times in the New Testament, all in the later Pauline epistles (Acts 17 and 2 Peter 1). In Acts 17:29, Paul uses it in his speech to the Athenians to affirm that God transcends material representations. In 2 Peter 1:3-4, the apostle Peter uses the same adjective and the noun to speak of God's saving power and the believers' participation in the divine nature — a central theme of the theology of spiritual transformation. The context emphasizes what God is and what He communicates to His own.
G2304.portee: This word reminds Christians that God is absolutely other, transcendent, and that His power and nature cannot be reduced to any human image or concept. It also affirms an extraordinary promise: the believer, through their relationship with Christ, is called to become a partaker of the divine nature, not by their own strength, but by the promises and power of God. It is a call to profound transformation and real communion with God.

sens: The divine nature of God, the sum of His attributes and characteristics that make Him divine
G2305.detail: 1. The word designates the divine nature itself — not God in person, but what makes Him divine: His attributes, His power, His majesty. In Romans 1:20, Paul says that this divinity of God is visible in His creations: when one contemplates the universe and its wonders, one discovers God's eternal power and invisible divinity. This is a teaching of natural revelation — God has made Himself known through His works.
G2305.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "divine" (theios). It designates the qualities and properties that constitute the divine nature — it is a quality or attribute of God rather than God Himself. Biblical Greek distinguishes it from "theotēs" (godhead, divine personality), which evokes the very essence of God.
G2305.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:20. Paul uses it to affirm that God's invisible attributes — His eternal power and divine nature — are recognizable in creation, visible to anyone who wishes to observe them. It is a theological argument: no one can claim to be ignorant of God, for He has manifested Himself in His work.
G2305.portee: This word reminds us that God is not hidden: His perfections become visible to those who contemplate creation with an attentive heart. The divinity of God is not an abstract doctrine, but a reality perceptible in the world He has created. This invites us to recognize God in His creation and to glorify Him for who He is.

sens: Which is composed of sulfur or resembles sulfur
Which has the characteristic pale yellow color of sulfur
Which emits an odor or smoke reminiscent of sulfur
Figuratively: which evokes divine judgment and infernal torments
G2306.detail: 1. The word primarily describes what is literally made of sulfur or contains it. In Revelation 9:17, the horses in the apocalyptic vision have breastplates of sulfur color, a distinctive pale yellow hue. 2. The adjective emphasizes this characteristic sulfur color: pale yellow, almost greenish, easily recognizable. The Bible often associates sulfur with destruction and punishment (as in Genesis 19:24, where the Lord rains down fire and sulfur on Sodom). 3. Sulfur in antiquity was known for its pungent smell when burned, and for the thick smoke it produces — hence its symbolic use to represent torment. 4. In the apocalyptic context, the “sulfur” horses with their breastplates of fire, smoke, and sulfur belching from their mouths (Revelation 9:17) embody the power of divine judgment: what smells of sulfur is the odor of condemnation.
G2306.origine: The adjective θειώδης derives from the Greek word θεῖον (theion), "sulfur." Sulfur is a yellowish mineral known since antiquity for its strong odor and flammable properties. The Greek word likely has a common root with the verb "to burn" or "to blaze." In Hebrew, the Old Testament refers to גָפְרִית (gofrit), sulfur, especially in accounts of divine destruction (Sodom, Gomorrah). Thus, sulfur becomes an essential symbol in the Bible of the fire of judgment and hell.
G2306.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 9:17, in the vision of the apocalyptic horses carrying riders clad in breastplates of colors of fire, hyacinth (blue-purple), and sulfur. It is a rare and highly symbolic term, used to intensify the horrifying and supernatural aspect of this eschatological vision. Sulfur embodies destructive divine judgment, an image that any biblical reader immediately recognizes from Old Testament accounts (Sodom, Gomorrah, Ezekiel 38:22).
G2306.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God's judgment is not an abstraction, but a reality with visible and terrifying signs. In Revelation 9, the description of the sulfur horses signals the irruption of the supernatural and the divine into history. It is an invitation to spiritual vigilance: sulfur evokes both the end times and the call to repentance before this judgment arrives.

sens: What a person wants, their desire, their decision
The power or right to decide something
The intention, order, or plan of someone
What is wished for, what must happen according to someone's plan
G2307.detail:
1. What a person wants, their desire, their decision: it is the act of wanting something. For example, in 1 Corinthians 16:12, Paul says that Apollos does not want to come now – it is his personal decision. John 1:13 speaks of those who are born "not of the will of the flesh," meaning not from human desire.
2. The power or right to decide: it is the right one has to do what one wants. In Luke 23:25, Pilate delivers Jesus to the will of the crowd – he lets them decide what they want to do with him.
3. The intention, order, or plan of someone: it is what someone has decided to do or have done. Acts 13:22 says that David will accomplish "all my wills" – the orders and plans of God.
4. What is wished for, what must happen according to someone's plan: it is the expected outcome, the intended goal. In Matthew 6:10, we ask God that His will be done on earth – that His plan be fulfilled.
G2307.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "to want" (thélo). Will is thus the action or state of wanting. In the Greek Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew "haphets" (the one who desires, who decides) and "ratson" (the one who wants, who agrees). It always involves the idea of choice and a person's decision.
G2307.emploi: This word appears 59 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles and in the Gospels. It primarily denotes human will: what we want to do, our desires and decisions (John 1:13, 1 Corinthians 16:12). But most uses refer to God's will: what God wants for us, His orders, His plan (Matthew 6:10, Romans 12:2, Ephesians 5:17). Jesus emphasizes the importance of fulfilling God's will (John 6:38, Hebrews 10:7). Paul also stresses that we must submit to God's plan and understand what He wants (Romans 12:2, Colossians 1:9). The word can refer to both momentary desire and a person's lasting plan.
G2307.portee: Understanding the meaning of the word "will" helps grasp a central question of the Christian life: how does my will align with God's? The Bible calls us not only to know what God wants but to do it (Matthew 7:21). This means abandoning our selfish plans to embrace God's plan. It is the path to peace and blessing (Romans 12:2).

sens: What someone wants to do or desires
The ability to want, to decide
The power of choice and decision
G2308.detail:
1. Will is what a person truly wants — their deep desire, their resolution. In Hebrews 2:4, the text speaks of the gifts of the Holy Spirit "distributed according to His will": this means that God Himself chooses how and to whom He gives these gifts, according to His sovereign decision.
2. The word also denotes the ability to want, to make a decision. It is the power to choose, to determine what one will do. When it is said that something is done "according to someone's will," it acknowledges that this person has the power and authority to decide.
3. More broadly, it is the exercise of free choice — the facet of ourselves that deliberates, weighs options, and ultimately decides. This Greek word thus expresses thoughtful intention and the power to act according to that intention.
G2308.origine: The word comes from the verb θέλω (thélō), "to want, to desire." It is a classical Greek term that expresses conscious and deliberate will, much deeper than a mere wish. The Hebrew רָצוֹן (ratzôn, "good pleasure, will"), often translated by this word in the Greek Old Testament, reinforces this idea: it is the sovereign will of the one who has the power to decide.
G2308.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament: in Hebrews 2:4. The author uses it to emphasize that God distributes the charisms — the gifts of the Holy Spirit — not randomly or according to a fixed system, but according to His own sovereign will. It is an affirmation of God's absolute authority and freedom in exercising His power. By choosing this specific term rather than another, the author highlights that it is a deliberate and thoughtful choice of God, not a mechanical distribution.
G2308.portee: This word reminds us that God does not depend on anyone for His decisions: He acts according to His own will. For the reader, this means that spiritual gifts are not rights that can be claimed, but presents that only God distributes according to His wisdom. This invites the Christian to humbly receive what God chooses to give him, and to respect divine sovereignty in the distribution of charisms in the Church.

sens: To have the will, the desire to do something
To wish for something to happen
To be willing to welcome or receive
To consent, to accept willingly
To ask, to demand
To manifest an intention or will through one's actions
G2309.detail:
1. To have the will or desire to do something: it is the movement of the soul towards an action. Joseph "did not want" to publicly disgrace Mary (Matthew 1:19): he had internally resolved not to do so. Jesus asks his disciples where they "want" him to prepare the Passover (Matthew 26:17), meaning what they wish.
2. To wish for something to happen or to be true: it is to desire a state, a situation. The Jews "wanted" to stone Jesus because he made himself out to be God (John 5:40, implicit in the context). This is also the meaning when one "wants" to be called by a certain name (Luke 1:62).
3. To be willing to welcome or receive: the disciples gave out fish "as much as they wanted" (John 6:11), meaning as much as they desired, as much as they asked for.
4. To consent, to accept willingly, especially in response to a request or demand: to refuse to want ("not wanting") is to reject, to push away. The king "did not want" (Matthew 18:30) to show mercy to the servant who begged him.
5. To ask, to demand something: when one says "what do you want?", one is asking what one wishes to receive or know.
6. To show through one's actions a will, a hidden intention: Paul says he has "the will" (Romans 7:18) to do good, but his sinful body prevents him. It is the internal capacity to want, even before action.
G2309.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses desire and consent. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to the verb "chaphatz" (חפץ), which means "to take pleasure in," "to approve," "to desire." It is a very common word in Greek to express personal will, more frequent than the verb "boulesthai" which emphasizes a more thoughtful decision. The reinforced form "ethelo" (ἐθέλω) also exists in ancient Greek.
G2309.emploi: The verb "vouloir" is used about two hundred times in the New Testament. It always denotes an act of will, desire, or consent. It can be found alone ("the Lord wanted it," Acts 18:21), with a direct object ("to want this or that"), with an infinitive ("to want to do"), or with a proposition ("to want that"). Paul uses it frequently to express the contrast between his will and his ability: he "wants" to do good but cannot (Romans 7:15-19). Jesus uses it to manifest the refusal of those who "do not want" to come to him (John 5:40). The word contrasts with actual action ("to do"): one can want without being able to realize it.
G2309.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine their own will in light of God's will. It shows that human will is real and responsible — one cannot reject Christ without refusing to want him — but also limited and sometimes in conflict with what one knows to be good. Understanding that one "wants" something helps to discern one's deep desires and to submit them to God's will, which alone liberates and saves.

sens: Stone or construction on which a building rests
Stable base or foundation on which something immaterial is built
What supports and remains firm
Jesus Christ as the foundation of the Church
The apostles and prophets as the foundation of faith
G2310.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the foundation is the set of stones or the underground structure that is dug and laid before building a house. Jesus tells that the one who builds "dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock" (Luke 6:48): without a solid foundation, the house collapses when the flood comes.

2. In the figurative sense, it is the base on which something is supported: Paul refuses "to build on someone else's foundation" (Romans 15:20), meaning to preach the Gospel in churches already established by other apostles.

3. Particularly in the Church, the foundation is what remains stable and unshakeable. Paul affirms that "the solid foundation of God stands firm" (2 Timothy 2:19), regardless of human weaknesses.

4. Jesus Christ is the unique foundation: "No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:11).

5. The Church is built "on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone" (Ephesians 2:20): the apostles and prophets form, with Jesus, the base on which God's people rest.
G2310.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to lay, to place" which evokes the action of putting something stable in place. In classical Greek, it literally designates the stone base of a building. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew words for "base," "foundation," or "dwelling" — the image is always that of a structure established solidly to last long.
G2310.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Luke uses it for the house built on the rock (6:48-49) and for the foundations of a tower (14:29). Paul uses it in a strongly figurative sense: in 1 Corinthians 3, he explains that Christ alone is the true foundation on which the Church is built, and that our work will be judged according to its quality. In Ephesians 2:20, the foundation includes the apostles and prophets with Christ. Hebrews 11:10 speaks of the foundations of the heavenly city. In Revelation 21, we see the twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem, adorned with precious stones. The word oscillates between the material sense (a construction) and the spiritual sense (what supports faith).
G2310.portee: This word reminds the Christian that all lasting spiritual life must rest on a solid base. If Jesus Christ is the only true foundation of the Church, then our faith must not rely on changing doctrines, human wisdom, or other religious leaders, but solely on him. The image of the foundation also invites us to dig deep, to build solidly in prayer and obedience, not lightly. Finally, it assures us that God's project stands firm: "the foundation of God remains standing."

sens: Establish the foundations of a house or a construction
Securely establish, anchor something or someone in a stable base
Root someone in a truth, a conviction, or a relationship in an unshakable manner
G2311.detail:
1. Literally, it means to lay the foundations of a building. Hebrews 1:10 applies it to creation: God "founded" the earth, just as one lays the foundations of a house. This image is concrete: without solid foundations, a house collapses.

2. Matthew 7:25 uses this image to speak of a house built on the rock — its foundations are solid, and it withstands storms. It is a symbol of stability in the face of trials.

3. Figuratively, "found" means to establish someone in a conviction or a relationship. Ephesians 3:17 speaks of being "rooted in love": having the love of Christ as the unshakable foundation of one's life. Colossians 1:23 says to be "grounded and steadfast in the faith" — faith becomes the solid base that prevents the believer from deviating.
G2311.origine: The word comes from θέμελος (themélos), which means "foundation, base." It is the image of a construction that starts from the lowest, the deepest: one digs, one lays the foundation stones. The image evokes solidity, stability, that which does not move. This root also appears in the French word "thème," which is the basis of a discourse.
G2311.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the passive voice (passive form: "to be founded"). Matthew and Luke use it for the house built on the rock — an image taught by Jesus. Hebrews applies it to creation itself: God founded the heavens and the earth. Paul uses it three times to speak of spiritual stability: being founded in love (Ephesians), in faith (Colossians), or made steadfast (1 Peter). The context is always that of solidity in the face of trials or variability.
G2311.portee: This word reminds the believer that it is not enough to start a relationship with God: solid foundations are necessary. These are the love of Christ and faith in the Gospel. This image of foundation invites us to examine what our spiritual life truly rests upon — on the rock of Christ, or on sand that collapses? It also encourages us to deepen, to dig down to the roots, rather than remaining on the surface.

sens: Instructed directly by God, without human intermediary
Who has received divine teaching in their heart
G2312.detail:
1. Taught by God describes a person whom God himself has instructed, without any human teacher intervening. It is a learning that comes directly from God, engraved in the believer's heart. In 1 Thessalonians 4:9, Paul tells the Christians in Thessalonica that they are "taught by God" in brotherly love: they do not need to be taught how to love one another, because God himself has put this love in their hearts.
2. This word evokes the idea of an inner and living knowledge, one that God communicates directly to the believing soul through His Spirit. It stands in contrast to purely external or bookish knowledge: it is a truth that the heart has learned and accepted.
G2312.origine: The word θεοδίδακτος is formed from two elements: θεο- ("God") and δίδακτος ("taught," from the verb δίδασκω, "to teach"). It describes one who has God as their teacher. In the Greek Old Testament, God is presented as the true Master who instructs His people through His Law and His Spirit: this is the image that this word expresses on a personal and spiritual level.
G2312.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in 1 Thessalonians 4:9. Paul uses it to encourage the Thessalonians in their brotherly love. He tells them that they do not need a letter or external instruction on this subject, for God himself has taught them — He has put love for one another in their hearts. This word expresses the conviction that the grace and Spirit of the Lord work directly in the believer's heart, beyond any human words.
G2312.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that true knowledge of God and His love does not come only from sermons or books, but from a direct action of the Holy Spirit in the heart. It encourages us to trust in what God is working intimately within us, without always waiting for external instruction. It is also a call to recognize that our brothers and sisters carry this divine teaching within them: we should respect them not because they are learned, but because God instructs them.

sens: Openly oppose God and His action
Actively resist the will of God
Act against divine purposes
G2313.detail:
1. Openly oppose God and His action: the word literally evokes a fight, an armed struggle against God Himself. It is a declared hostility, not mere silent disobedience. In Acts 23:9, the Pharisees warn the Sadducees: "And if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?" — they refuse to fight against what might come from God, recognizing that one cannot oppose God with impunity.
2. Actively resist the will of God: it is to take up arms against His authority, refusing to obey Him not out of weakness but out of deliberate hostility. It is a conscious choice of confrontation.
3. Act against divine purposes: to fight against God ultimately means to work against His plans, His salvation, His justice — a folly since no one can defeat the Almighty.
G2313.origine: The word is composed of "God" (theos) and "fight" (machê). It literally designates a fight against God. It is a rare word that emphasizes the absurdity of any resistance against the Almighty: this is why the Pharisees in Acts refuse to enter into this struggle.
G2313.emploi: The verb appears only once in common translations of the New Testament, in Acts 23:9. Paul stands before the Sanhedrin; the Pharisees and Sadducees confront each other over the question of resurrection. A Pharisee exclaims: "Let us not fight against God!" — recognizing that if Paul has truly received a divine vision, opposing it would be suicidal folly. The word thus expresses a prudent wisdom: it is better to withdraw from a struggle that could put you at war with heaven.
G2313.portee: This word reminds the believer of the absurdity of any rebellion against God. It is a warning against the pride that leads one to consciously resist His plans. It also invites us to recognize, within the Church, when a testimony or work truly comes from God, rather than opposing it out of fear or traditionalism.

sens: To oppose God through actions or words
To resist God's plan and His work
To be an active adversary of God
G2314.detail:
1. The word describes one who engages in direct combat against God, like a warrior facing an enemy. It is an active and declared opposition, not mere passive unbelief. In Acts 5:39, the apostles warn the Sanhedrin that by persecuting the disciples, they risk literally "fighting against God." 
2. More broadly, it is to resist the work of the Holy Spirit and God's plan for humanity. One who "fights against God" opposes His saving purposes. It is to pretend to be able to stop or annihilate what God wants to accomplish — an endeavor doomed to failure. 
3. The word carries the idea of a lost battle from the start: how could a creature defeat its Creator? This is why the apostles' warning is so serious: do not place yourself in this impossible and destructive position.
G2314.origine: The Greek word combines θεός (theos, "God") and the verb μάχομαι (machomai, "to fight," "to struggle"). It literally expresses the fight of a warrior. This image evokes the folly of human pride: to pretend to fight against God is like a lone soldier standing against an invincible army.
G2314.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:39, in the speech of the wise Gamaliel to the Sanhedrin. It designates one who would actively oppose God's action through the nascent Church. It is a serious term, highlighting the spiritual stakes of rejecting the Gospel: it is not a human matter, but a matter of God Himself. The context shows that it is a veiled threat and a call for caution: the Sanhedrin risks placing itself on the wrong side.
G2314.portee: This word calls the believer to a clear conscience: there is a spiritual reality engaged in every choice faced with the Gospel. Rejecting or persecuting God's work is not a neutral or political matter; it is a fight against God Himself — a position ultimately untenable. For one who follows Jesus, it is also an assurance: one who defends God's cause will fight with Him, and this cause cannot be destroyed.

sens: Coming from God, produced by divine breath
Carrying the authority and truth of God
Not of human origin but divine
G2315.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of God's breath that "inspires" — that brings His own word into us. It is as if God Himself breathed His thoughts into the authors, leading them to write without stripping them of their personality. In 2 Timothy 3:16, Paul uses it for all Scripture: "All Scripture is God-breathed," affirming that every passage comes from divine breath. 
2. A God-breathed text is not merely an excellent human writing. It carries divine authority itself and therefore cannot err in what it asserts. This is why Paul immediately adds that this "God-breathed" Scripture is "useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction" — it possesses transformative power. 
3. The word rejects a false opposition: it is neither a mechanically dictated text nor a mere improved human book. It is a work where God acts through His Spirit, guaranteeing the reliability of the message without destroying the freedom or unique style of each author.
G2315.origine: The Greek word combines "God" (θεός) and the verb "to breathe" (πνέω), hence "breathed by God." This image of breath comes from the Hebrew Old Testament: the "Spirit of God" (Ruach Elohim) in Genesis 1:2 or 2 Samuel 23:2 ("The Spirit of the Lord spoke by me"). The word theopneustos was a Christian creation to express what was implicitly affirmed in Hebrew Scripture: that God Himself is the source of prophetic word.
G2315.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:16, where Paul uses it to solemnly affirm the nature of Scripture. This rarity shows that it is a capital affirmation: Paul seeks the exact word to say that Scripture is not a human production, but divine. The context (vv. 14-17) confirms this: Timothy has known the Scriptures since childhood, and Paul exhorts him to hold firmly to them as useful words "for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness." Inspiration is never presented as magical or abnormal, but as the means by which God has guaranteed the reliability and usefulness of His word.
G2315.portee: This affirmation grounds the believer's trust in Scripture. If it is truly "God-breathed" and not of human origin, it does not deceive us and deserves our obedience. It also tells us that we can rely on it for our faith, correction, and instruction — these are not merely venerable ancient texts, but the living word of God for today. Finally, this invites us to receive the Bible, not as a mere literary monument, but as the voice of God speaking to us.

sens: Divine being, deity in a polytheistic religious system
The one true and unique God, creator and sovereign of heaven and earth
The one who knows hearts and judges with justice
The one who forgives and grants grace to those who believe
The divine person in Himself, in His essence and nature
G2316.detail:
1. The word θεός primarily designates, in a general sense, any superhuman being revered as divine: the Acts report that the inhabitants of Lystra believed that Paul and Barnabas were gods (Acts 14:11). Paul also writes to the Galatians that formerly, not knowing God, they served gods that are not really gods (Galatians 4:8). 

2. But in the Bible, θεός especially designates the true, unique, and personal God. It is the God of Israel, creator of heaven and earth, whom Jesus calls "my Father." He is presented as living, acting, and speaking: "God with us" (Matthew 1:23), He makes the flowers of the field grow without them toiling (Matthew 6:30). 

3. God sees the hearts of men and judges with justice. Jesus says that nothing escapes God: "God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers" (Hebrews 13:4), and Paul reminds that "no flesh may boast before God" (1 Corinthians 1:29). 

4. God is also the one who saves and forgives. Jesus teaches that whoever comes to Him will be saved: "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" (Matthew 19:26). He grants His favor to those who believe in Him (Acts 16:34). 

5. When the Bible speaks of "the will of God" or "the word of God," it designates the very essence of God, His character and intentions: what He wants, what He says, what He commands. This is why the apostles do "the will of God from the heart" (Ephesians 6:6).
G2316.origine: The word θεός comes from an Indo-European root expressing the divine or the luminous atmosphere (whence "god" in French, "deus" in Latin, "Gott" in German). In the Greek Old Testament, θεός primarily translates the Hebrew word אֱלֹהִים (Elohim), which designates both the God of Israel and, by extension, any superhuman or divine being. It is a fundamental word in the biblical language, used over 1,300 times in the New Testament alone.
G2316.emploi: The word θεός appears about 1,300 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Paul's Epistles. It is used in two distinct senses: the polytheistic sense (the gods of the pagans) and the monotheistic sense (the unique God). In the Gospels, it designates the God that Jesus reveals as His Father — the one who loves sinners, who heals, who forgives, who will judge. In Paul, God is presented as the source of all grace and justification by faith. The word often appears without an article ("God so loved") or with the definite article ("the God of your fathers"), depending on the context and theological nuance. Its use culminates in the confessions of faith: "Jesus is the Son of God" (Matthew 16:16).
G2316.portee: For the Christian, this word expresses the central reality of faith: that there is a personal, living, just, and good God who knows every heart and demands faith and obedience. It is through the relationship with this God that one finds meaning, forgiveness, and eternal life. Understanding that God is the one who sees, who judges fairly, and who forgives — this transforms the way faith is lived out daily.

sens: reverential respect for God
sincere desire to please God and live according to His will
true piety expressed through conduct and actions
G2317.detail:
1. The fear of God refers to the deep and reverential respect one has for God — not a paralyzing fear, but the honor and veneration inspired by His majesty. It is the attitude of one who recognizes God's greatness and sovereign authority.
2. It manifests itself through a sincere desire to please God and live according to His will, seeking to do what is right and good. It is a heart oriented towards God, a faithfulness of the heart.
3. This fear is concretely expressed through an exemplary life and good works: in 1 Timothy 2:10, the Apostle Paul urges women who "profess to serve God" to adorn themselves with good works, for this is the true expression of their fear of God — piety is not just spoken, it is lived.
G2317.origine: The Greek word is formed from "theos" (God) and "sebeia" (reverence, respect), hence its literal meaning of "reverence towards God." This fear is not an innovation of the New Testament: it takes up the classical Hebrew idea of "the fear of the Lord," present in the Old Testament (notably in Proverbs) where it is described as "the beginning of wisdom." Ancient Greek translations (the Septuagint) use this word to render the Hebrew terms denoting respectful fear of God.
G2317.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:10, where Paul uses it in an ethical exhortation context. He urges Christian women to cultivate a true fear of God that is not limited to beautiful clothing, but is expressed through acts of kindness and virtue. The use of the term shows that Christian piety is never purely internal: it must shine through concrete conduct, visible to all. It is a call to moral and spiritual authenticity.
G2317.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that true faith is not a matter of words or appearances, but a matter of the heart that unfolds in concrete actions. The fear of God invites us to respect His majesty, to desire to please Him, and to let this conviction transform our daily lives. It is an invitation to coherence: that our works reflect our love for God.

sens: who fears and respects God
who lives according to God's will
G2318.detail:
1. The word designates someone who fears God — not a servile fear, but deep respect and reverence towards the Lord. It is piety in action: one who recognizes God's power and authority and submits to it. In John 9:31, the healed blind man states: "God does not hear sinners; but if anyone honors Him and does His will, He hears him." The verb "honor" translates our word here: to honor God is to fear Him with respect.
2. The one who fears God lives according to His will. It is not a mere emotion, but a way of life: it is acting with the intention of pleasing God, obeying His commandments. The fear of God produces righteous conduct.
G2318.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: θεός (theos, "God") and σέβομαι (sebomai, "to honor, to revere"). It literally expresses the idea of honoring God. In Hebrew, the Old Testament speaks of the same spiritual state with the expression "fear God" (יָרֵא אֱלֹהִים). This word is close to the term εὐσεβής (eusebès, "pious"), but emphasizes respectful fear more than general piety.
G2318.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 9:31. It is the man born blind, miraculously healed by Jesus, who uses it to describe the one whom God listens to. In this context of tension with the Pharisees, who do not recognize Jesus, the blind man recalls a simple spiritual truth: God hears those who fear Him and do His will, not those who live in sin. It is an affirmation of faith in divine justice.
G2318.portee: This word reminds the reader that the relationship with God is based on fear and respect — not through terror, but through sincere recognition of His authority. The one who fears God is not someone who dreads Him as a tyrant, but someone who orients their entire life around His will. It is an invitation to examine one's own conduct: do we live genuinely seeking to please God and obey Him?

sens: Who is hated by God, cursed by Him
Who hates God, who rejects Him with hostility
G2319.detail:
1. The word can first designate one who is the object of God's hatred — someone so perverted, so hostile to divine order, that God Himself rejects them. It conveys the idea of a cursed person, abominable in the eyes of the Creator. In Romans 1:30, the Apostle Paul lists the vices of men who have rejected God, and "wicked" is among the traits of those who refuse to acknowledge their Creator.

2. The word can also mean actively: one who hates God, who consciously and hostilely rejects Him. It is the person who does not merely ignore God, but who fights against Him, denies Him, despises Him — an explicit revolt against His authority and holiness.
G2319.origine: The Greek word is composed of θεός (theos, "God") and στυγέω (stugéo, "to hate, to abhor"). It literally designates one who hates God or who is hated by God. This dual possibility of meaning — passive and active — is common in ancient Greek: a word formed from an action can express both the one who undergoes it and the one who performs it. The root στυγέω is linked to the idea of repulsion, of deep disgust.
G2319.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Romans 1:30. Paul places it in a blacklist of vices characterizing the pagans who have closed their eyes to God's revelation in creation. Alongside "gossips," "slanderers," "arrogant," "haughty," he describes the fundamental attitude of rebellion against God — whether one actively hates Him or has become abominable. The context shows that Paul speaks of a systematic refusal to recognize and honor the Creator, leading to total moral impurity.
G2319.portee: This word reminds the reader that the rejection of God is never neutral: it manifests a deep hostility towards the Creator. The Apostle thus invites the Christian to recognize the seriousness of sin — not merely as error or weakness, but as active revolt against the One from whom life has been received. It is also a call to gratitude: in Christ, we have passed from this cursed state to reconciliation with God.

sens: divine nature of God
complete divine essence
reality of what is God
G2320.detail:
1. Divinity refers to what makes God, God: His divine nature, what distinguishes Him from all creation. In Colossians 2:9, Paul affirms that "all the fullness of the divinity" dwells in Christ bodily, meaning that Christ fully possesses the divine reality, the very essence of God.
2. It encompasses all the attributes and reality that constitute God: His power, His holiness, His eternity, His infinite knowledge. The word evokes less the acts of God than the very being of God in its totality.
G2320.origine: The word θεότης (theotēs) comes from θεός (theos), "God," to which the suffix -ότης (-otēs) is added, indicating a quality or essence. It literally means "the quality of being God" or "the state of divinity." There is a very similar word, θειότης (theiotes), which has a similar meaning but is rarely encountered.
G2320.emploi: The word θεότης appears only once in the New Testament: in Colossians 2:9. In this passage, the Apostle Paul refutes false doctrines that claimed Christ was merely a creature or an intermediary between God and men. Paul insists that it is in Christ that "all the fullness of the divinity" resides: not just a part or an image of God, but the totality of what God is. This context shows that Paul uses this word to express the complete and irreducible divine identity of Christ.
G2320.portee: This word speaks to us of the central mystery of the Christian faith: Jesus Christ is truly God, not a demigod or an intermediary. Understanding that "all the fullness of the divinity" dwells in Him assures us that we worship the true God by worshiping Christ, and that in Him we have access to the fullness of God Himself. It is a powerful word that invites the believer to recognize in Jesus the complete divine reality.

sens: Recipient of the two books of Luke (Gospel and Acts)
High-ranking individual honored by Luke
G2321.detail: Theophilus is the name of the person to whom the evangelist Luke directly addresses his Gospel and the book of Acts. Luke refers to him as "most excellent Theophilus" in Luke 1:3, indicating that he is a person of high social rank, possibly a magistrate or a Roman official. In Acts 1:1, Luke mentions Theophilus again to remind him that he is continuing the account he had already addressed to him, thus providing continuity between the two books.
G2321.origine: The Greek name Θεόφιλος (Theophilos) comes from two words: θεός (theos, God) and φίλος (philos, friend or beloved). It literally means "friend of God" or "beloved of God." It was a common Greek name in antiquity. Here, Luke chooses not to give the full name of this individual with other titles, but simply addresses him respectfully.
G2321.emploi: Theophilus appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the writings of Luke: once in the prologue of the Gospel according to Luke (1:3) and once at the beginning of the book of Acts (1:1). This repetition shows that Luke composes these two books as a two-part work intended for the same reader. Although some have speculated about the historical identity of Theophilus, the Bible provides no further information about him. He likely represents a believer or a friend of the faith to whom Luke wants to convey an orderly and reliable account of the life of Jesus and the beginnings of the Church.

sens: Care and restoration of health
Service rendered, assistance
All the servants and people of a household
G2322.detail:
1. Healing is the restoration of health, the act of treating a sick person. In Luke 9:11, Jesus heals those who needed healing, meaning he restores health to those who lacked it. In Revelation 22:2, the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations, to restore them spiritually.
2. More broadly, it refers to the service rendered to someone, the help or assistance provided to them. The word evokes the attention a servant gives to his master.
3. By extension, it designates all the servants or people in the service of a household: in Luke 12:42, the master appoints a steward over his "servants" to feed them — referring to the domestic staff.
G2322.origine: The word comes from the verb "therapeuō" which means "to serve" or "to care for." Originally, it evokes the idea of taking care of someone, as a servant looks after his master. In Hebrew, it often translates the word "eved" (עֶבֶד) which designates a servant or domestic. The medical sense of healing developed from this central idea of caring for, serving by restoring health.
G2322.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Luke 9:11, it specifically refers to the act of healing the sick. In Luke 12:42, it takes on the meaning of domestic staff, the people of a household that need to be fed. In Revelation 22:2, it returns to the sense of healing, but spiritual, for the nations. The word thus oscillates between the concrete idea of service (in the sense of domesticity) and the idea of restoring health, both meanings sharing the common root of "taking care of."
G2322.portee: This word reminds us that healing is not a magical power, but an act of service and love towards the suffering. For Jesus, to heal is to serve. For the Christian, it invites us to see every care given to a sick brother as a form of service rendered to Christ himself. The final image of the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations speaks of hope: there is complete restoration, a definitive healing in heaven.

sens: To treat a disease or infirmity
To care for a sick person, to deliver them from their physical ailment
To restore someone to health
To cast out an evil spirit or demon causing the illness
To render service, to serve (first and rare meaning)
G2323.detail:
1. The word designates the action of treating a disease or infirmity, to care for it in order to heal. This is the medical sense of the term: to restore the health of a sick body. In Matthew 4:23, Jesus goes throughout Galilee "healing every disease and every infirmity."
2. Concretely, this means to treat a sick person, to act on them to deliver them from their ailment. Mark 6:13 reports that the disciples "anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them."
3. The word can also refer to the result: to restore health, to put an end to physical suffering. Luke 8:2 speaks of women "who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities."
4. In several passages, to heal means to cast out a demon or an evil spirit that causes illness. Luke 7:21 shows Jesus healing "many people of diseases and plagues, and of evil spirits."
5. Rarely, the word carries the broader meaning of "to render service" or "to serve": this appears in Acts 17:25, where Paul says that God "is not served by human hands."
G2323.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of "to serve" or "to take care of." In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it often translates the Hebrew "ravah" and other verbs of healing. The medical sense developed gradually: first "to care for, to take care of," then specialized into "to heal a disease." It is a common word in Greek medical terminology and in the writings of physicians.
G2323.emploi: The word appears 43 times in the New Testament, mostly in the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John). It describes the healing activity of Jesus, which is at the heart of his ministry: Matthew, Mark, and Luke report it continuously. The disciples also receive the power to heal (Matthew 10:8, Luke 9:1). The word is used for miraculous healings (paralyzed, blind, possessed) and sometimes for the expulsion of demons. After Pentecost, the apostles perform healings (Acts 4:14, 5:16). The context is almost always one of relief and restoration: healing manifests the power and compassion of Jesus.
G2323.portee: This word reveals that healing is not for the Bible a simple technical repair of the body: it is an act of compassion and divine power. Jesus heals because he loves and because he has authority over evil. These healings are never separated from faith and love. For the Christian, seeing how Jesus heals calls us to do the same for the suffering, with the same gaze of tenderness.

sens: One who serves in a household, who waits on someone
A figure of authority and trust in a home
One who renders service faithfully and devotedly
G2324.detail:
1. A servant is someone who works for another person, serving and waiting on them. It is a human or social status: one who carries out tasks, obeys orders, and provides service in a household or community.
2. This word also carries a nuance of dignity and trust: it refers to a reliable servant, to whom the master entrusts important responsibilities. Moses is called a "servant" in Hebrews 3:5, not as a slave but as a trustworthy man in God's house, worthy of honor because he fulfills his mission faithfully.
3. The service described here is a vocation: the servant does not serve out of fear or force, but by accepting their place and fulfilling it with dedication. It is a form of voluntary and conscious service.
G2324.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the action of serving and waiting. In Hebrew, it corresponds mainly to "עֶבֶד" (eved), which designates the servant in the Old Testament. This family of words always depicts the relationship between the one who serves and the one who is served, a relationship that can be servile or, conversely, marked by fidelity and honor.
G2324.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 3:5. The author uses it to describe Moses as a faithful servant in God's house. This context shows that the word does not speak of degrading submission, but of the honorable position of a man chosen to fulfill a divine mission. Moses was faithful in all God's house, which means he loyally executed what was entrusted to him, distinguishing him from a mere servant: he is a trustworthy servant, a mediator between God and His people.
G2324.portee: This word reminds us that faithful service, regardless of our position, is honorable in God's eyes. Moses, despite his greatness, is described as a servant: this shows that faithfulness to the mission God entrusts to us is more important than title or glory. For every believer, it is an invitation to humbly accept our role in God's house and to fulfill it with dedication.

sens: To gather and harvest ripe grains from a field
To reap the fruit of one's labor
To obtain the result of one's actions or conduct
To reap what one has not sown oneself
G2325.detail:
1. To harvest means to gather the grains that have reached maturity in a field — this is the concrete image of the word. The birds of the air do not harvest (Matthew 6:26), for they do not work to cultivate a harvest: this work belongs to man.
2. By extension, to harvest means to reap the fruit of one's labor. He who sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and he who sows generously will reap generously (2 Corinthians 9:6): the agricultural image becomes the symbol of the reward that corresponds to the effort.
3. The word takes on a moral sense: to harvest means to obtain the result of one's actions, what one has sown before. He who sows corruption will reap corruption; he who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life (Galatians 6:8).
4. Sometimes, one harvests what one has not sown — which means benefiting from the work of others. The disciples are sent to harvest without having worked for the seed: others have sown before them (John 4:38).
G2325.origine: The Greek word comes from a root related to "summer" (θέρος), the season of harvest in the Mediterranean world. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew קָצַר (qaçar), which also means "to cut, to harvest." It is a word deeply rooted in the agricultural experience of the people of the Bible.
G2325.emploi: The verb to harvest appears 17 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Luke, and Paul. Initially used in a concrete sense (Matthew 6:26: the birds do not harvest), it quickly becomes figurative: it designates the spiritual result of an action. Paul uses it to express the correspondence between sowing and reaping (2 Corinthians 9:6, Galatians 6:7-9), thus rooting Christian morality in the natural order. In John, the word describes the disciples' engagement in God's work: they harvest the fruit of the work of Jesus and those who preceded Him (John 4:36-38). Revelation uses the image to describe the final judgment (Revelation 14:15-16).
G2325.portee: This word reminds Christians of an undeniable law: we reap what we sow. It is a word that comforts those who work for God, even without immediately seeing the fruit (John 4:36), and warns those who would live in injustice or selfishness. It also invites gratitude: we often inherit the work of other faithful ones who have gone before us. Finally, it roots morality in nature itself, accessible to every believer.

sens: The action and moment of harvesting ripe grains
The time of year when this harvest takes place
The grains themselves once cut and gathered
The entirety of the work, the workers, and the result of the harvest
Spiritual image: the end of the world and God's judgment
Spiritual image: souls to be won for the Gospel
G2326.detail:
1. The harvest is primarily the act of gathering: cutting the ripe ears of wheat or barley with a sickle (Mark 4:29 says, "as soon as the fruit is ripe, he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come"). It is the moment when the grain, now golden and dry, is ready to be picked.
2. The word also designates the fixed time, the season when this work is done — generally in spring or summer depending on the regions. Matthew 13:30 refers to "the time of harvest" as a decisive moment that is approaching.
3. The harvest can also refer to the wheat itself once harvested, the entirety of the grain collected and ready to be stored (Matthew 13:30: "gather the wheat into my barn").
4. The term sometimes encompasses the entire process: fields covered with ripe ears, workers who labor, sheaves that are bound, and the final result. Matthew 9:37-38 speaks of "the harvest" as all this collective work that requires many hands.
5. Jesus uses the harvest to speak of the end times and judgment: "the harvest is the end of the world" and the angels are "the reapers" who will separate the righteous from the wicked (Matthew 13:39, Revelation 14:15).
6. The image also becomes that of souls to be saved: "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few" (Matthew 9:37); the disciples and evangelists are the workers who gather hearts for the Kingdom.
G2326.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "therízô" (to cut, to harvest) and refers to the Hebrew verb "qatsar" which means to cut, to remove (hence the Hebrew "qatsir" = harvest). The root evokes the concrete action of cutting and removing: one cuts, separating the ripe grain from the rest. The Greek word is used in the Greek translations of the Old Testament to translate this agricultural Hebrew vocabulary, naturally loaded with spiritual meaning.
G2326.emploi: The word "harvest" appears 13 times in the Segond, mainly in the Gospels. Matthew and Luke make it the central image of the apostolic mission (Matthew 9:37-38, Luke 10:2): the white field leaning toward the sickle becomes the symbol of the world ready to receive the Gospel. Matthew 13:30 and 39 link the harvest to the word and the end times — the sown grain germinates and must be separated at the final harvest. Mark 4:29 emphasizes the moment of ripe fruit: when everything is ready, the sickle comes into action. John 4:35 invites us to lift our eyes to the "white fields of harvest," an image of spiritual urgency. Revelation 14:15 takes up the eschatological motif with the reaping angels.
G2326.portee: The harvest teaches the believer that spiritual growth has a term, a moment of maturity when God acts. It urges them not to wait passively: there are workers to raise, work to be done before the moment passes. It also reminds us that all final judgment depends solely on God, but that every believer is invited to participate in the gathering of souls — not by their own strength, but in obedience to the Lord's call.

sens: One who gathers crops by cutting the ears of grain
Figuratively: the angel who executes God's judgment at the end of times
G2327.detail:
1. The harvester is the agricultural worker who gathers wheat or other grains by cutting them. In the parable of the wheat and the tares, Jesus speaks of the "harvesters" who work in the field and can be tasked during the harvest: "First gather the tares" (Matthew 13:30).
2. Jesus then explains the parable by revealing that the "harvesters" are not ordinary men, but the angels themselves. At the end of the world, they will sort the righteous from the wicked: "the harvesters are the angels" (Matthew 13:39). The image of the harvester becomes that of a celestial being who carries out divine judgment.
G2327.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "therizo" which means "to harvest," "to gather." This verb itself evokes the action of cutting or slicing the grain. The suffix "-tes" creates an agent noun, one who performs the action: the harvester. It is a simple word from peasant life, transformed by Jesus into an image of eschatological judgment.
G2327.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Gospel of Matthew, in Matthew 13:30 and 13:39, both in the parable and its explanation. Jesus first speaks of the harvesters as workers in the field (Matthew 13:30), then reveals in the explanation that they are the angels (Matthew 13:39). This passage is the only one in the New Testament where Jesus uses this agricultural image to refer to celestial beings who execute His final judgment on humanity.
G2327.portee: This image of the harvester invites the reader to see the final judgment not merely as destruction, but as a harvest: God discerns and gathers what belongs to Him. It also reminds us that it is God, through His angels, who has the final word on each person's fate, and that any premature judgment is not fitting for us. For the Christian, it is an invitation to persevere until the end and to leave to God alone the task of separating the good from the bad.

sens: To warm oneself by approaching the fire or heat
To provide warmth, to warm someone
To offer conditions for physical well-being without truly acting
G2328.detail:
1. The primary meaning is purely physical: to warm oneself by a source of heat. Peter, after his arrest, sits with the servants around a fire (John 18:18) to protect himself from the cold. It is the mundane action of seeking warmth for comfort.

2. The verb can also mean "to warm someone" in an active sense, providing them with the necessary warmth. In James 2:16, telling someone "warm yourselves" would be wishing them to get warm, but without giving them the real means to do so.

3. Spiritually, the word takes on a broader significance: it denotes the well-being of the body that one claims to ensure through hollow fine words. James uses it to show the absurdity of pious wishes — saying "warm yourselves and be filled" — without meeting concrete needs, is hypocrisy.
G2328.origine: The word comes from the Greek thermós (θερμός), which means "warm." In ancient Hebrew, it often corresponds to the image of being warm or warming up (חָמַם, hamam). Warmth was an image of comfort, life, real help — and by extension, the absence of aid when one pretends to help without acting.
G2328.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, and in all cases in the middle voice (the form that means "to warm oneself"). Four occurrences are concentrated in the account of Jesus' arrest: Peter warms himself around the fire in the high priest's courtyard, three times (Mark 14:54, 67; John 18:18, 25). It is in this context of the cold night and anxious waiting that Peter denies Jesus. A fifth occurrence, in James 2:16, steps out of this context: it uses the verb figuratively to show the futility of wishes without action.
G2328.portee: At the simplest levels: the word reminds us that bodily needs are real and legitimate — one must warm oneself when it is cold. But in James, it teaches that fine words without concrete action are vain and cruel lies. This passage questions the reader: does my faith translate into actions, or am I like one who says "warm yourselves" without giving anything?

sens: High temperature, sensation of warmth
Effect of combustion or fire
G2329.detail:
1. Heat is the sensation of warmth, the high temperature that emanates from a source of fire or sun. It is a simple, concrete physical reality: when one approaches the fire, one feels its effects. In Acts 28:3, after a shipwreck, Paul gathers wood to make a fire, and it is precisely the heat emitted by this fire that causes a viper hidden in the brush to come out — the reptile fled from the high temperature.
2. The word more broadly designates the action of fire that radiates and warms. It is thermal energy as a concrete and sensible phenomenon.
G2329.origine: The Greek thermē comes from an ancient root that expresses the idea of warmth and flame. The same family is found in thermos ("warm" in Greek) and in the French "thermes" (hot baths). This word often translates the Hebrew hamam (חָמַם), which also means "warm" or "to be heated." It is a simple, concrete word, without abstraction.
G2329.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:3. Luke uses it to describe a dramatic moment in Paul's journey after the shipwreck in Malta: the heat of the rekindled fire that brings the viper out of its refuge. It is a word from everyday vocabulary, without particular theological connotation — just the physical reality of heat.
G2329.portee: This passage reminds us that even when everything seems to go wrong — a shipwreck, an unknown island — God watches over His servant. The viper, instead of killing Paul, fails to truly harm him (verse 5). For the believer, it is an image of divine help in trials: God does not leave us without protection.

sens: The warm season of the year, between spring and autumn
(figuratively) the proximity of an awaited or dreaded reality
G2330.detail:
1. Summer is the hottest season of the year, when trees bear their fruit. In the Gospel, Jesus speaks of the fig tree that puts forth its leaves in summer (Matthew 24:32; Mark 13:28; Luke 21:30): it is the time of maturity and fertility in nature.
2. Jesus uses summer to signify the proximity of what is to come — "when you see these things, know that the kingdom of God is near" (Luke 21:30). Just as the leaf that grows announces the approaching summer, the signs He enumerates announce the fulfillment of His word. Summer thus becomes the image of what is inevitable and imminent.
G2330.origine: The Greek word theros comes from a root that means "to heat" (therô). It is a simple, concrete word that naturally designates the season of the blazing sun. The Hebrew of the Old Testament uses the word qaïts to name this season, and that is what theros translates. The word has retained its primary meaning and has no specific spiritual nuances: these must be sought in the context.
G2330.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, and always in the first three Gospels. Each time, Jesus uses it in a parable or teaching: He speaks of the fig tree that shows its leaves in summer (Matthew 24:32; Mark 13:28; Luke 21:30). It is a teaching about the signs of the times, where summer plays the role of a certain and imminent reality announced by a precursor sign. The word thus remains always concrete — the actual season of the year — but Jesus uses it for an eschatological lesson.
G2330.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that our faith is based on concrete and natural signs. Just as summer inevitably follows spring, so God's promise will be fulfilled with certainty. It is an invitation to vigilance and trust: recognizing the signs of the times is to prepare for the coming of the Lord with clarity and hope.

sens: inhabitant or native of Thessalonica
member of the Christian Church established in Thessalonica
G2331.detail:
1. A Thessalonian is a person from the city of Thessalonica, a major port city in Macedonia (in northern Greece). This is the name borne by Aristarchus in Acts 27:2, designated as "Macedonian from Thessalonica."

2. In Paul's epistles, the term primarily refers to the members of the Christian Church that Paul founded in Thessalonica during his second missionary journey. In 1 Thessalonians 1:1, Paul writes "to the Church of the Thessalonians," meaning the converts from this city who now form a community of faith. The term becomes almost synonymous with "Christians from Thessalonica."
G2331.origine: The word comes from Θεσσαλονίκη (Thessalonica), the Greek name of the city. The suffix -εύς (-eus) is a classical Greek ending that designates the inhabitant or native of a place, like Athenian (from Athens) or Corinthian (from Corinth). This type of formation is very common in Greek for forming demonyms.
G2331.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, exclusively in Acts and the two epistles to the Thessalonians. In Acts 20:4 and 27:2, it refers to Aristarchus and Sopater, traveling companions of Paul from Thessalonica. But it is especially in 1 Thessalonians 1:1 and 2 Thessalonians 1:1 that the term takes on its full significance: Paul uses it to address his epistles to the Church he planted there. The context shows that these Christians from Thessalonica formed a living community, and Paul writes specifically to encourage and instruct them in the faith.
G2331.portee: For today's Christian, discovering this term reminds us that faith is not abstract: it takes root in real cities, among real people. The Thessalonians show us that a local Church is a group of living believers, with their joys and struggles, worthy of being addressed with tenderness and authority. The two epistles addressed to them testify to Paul's personal interest in the well-being of his converts and the importance of community life in God's plan.

sens: Major city in Macedonia, important port on the Aegean Sea
Center of Jewish life and thriving commerce in northern Greece
Place where Paul founded a young church and addressed two epistles
G2332.detail: 1. Thessalonica is an important city in Macedonia (the northern region of present-day Greece), located on the port of the Aegean Sea. It is a prosperous commercial center with a strong Jewish presence: it has at least one synagogue where Jews gather for prayer and study of the Scriptures (Acts 17:1). 2. The city is the starting point of the opposition to Paul's preaching: when he announces Jesus there, some Jews become hostile and, learning that he will preach elsewhere, they follow him to stir up the crowds against him (Acts 17:13). 3. Despite this opposition, a church forms there and becomes so faithful and generous that the Thessalonians support Paul financially, even when he is elsewhere (Philippians 4:16), and some of Paul's companions like Demas eventually return there (2 Timothy 4:10).
G2332.origine: The name Thessalonica literally means "victory of Thessa[lus]" or comes from Greek mythology. The city was founded in the 4th century B.C. and is named after a Macedonian queen. It is a Greek city of primary importance, a center of commerce and religious life, hence its significance in Paul's missionary journey.
G2332.emploi: Thessalonica appears five times in the New Testament, always in contexts related to Paul. Paul arrives there during his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1) and preaches in the synagogue, generating both faith among converts and hostility among unbelieving Jews. The city is home to a young and enthusiastic Christian community to which Paul writes two epistles (1 and 2 Thessalonians). The generosity of this church is noted: it helps Paul several times, even in poverty (Philippians 4:16). It represents in Acts a crossroads where the Good News provokes both conversion and opposition.
G2332.portee: Thessalonica shows how the Gospel creates a living and generous community, capable of enduring persecution and supporting the missionary work despite poverty. It is also a place where the systematic opposition of religious authorities to the announcement of Jesus is manifested, but which cannot stop the growth of the church. For the reader, this city embodies the cost and joy of following Christ in the midst of a hostile world.

sens: Jewish leader who claimed to be the Messiah
Political and religious agitator of the 1st century
G2333.detail:
1. Theudas was a Jewish false messiah who appeared in Judea before the revolt of 66 A.D. He presented himself as something significant, likely claiming to be the messenger of God that the Jews were waiting for. About four hundred men followed him, seduced by his promises.
2. He was an agitator who incited an armed rebellion against Roman authority. The Roman governor had him executed, and his revolt collapsed: all his supporters were scattered and crushed, showing that his movement did not have the strength he claimed to possess.
G2333.origine: The name Theudas appears only once in the New Testament. The historian Josephus also mentions him in his accounts of 1st century Judea. This name may derive from a Greek diminutive, but its exact etymology remains debated. It has no direct Hebrew equivalent since it is a Greek name borne by a Jew of that time.
G2333.emploi: Theudas appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 5:36, where the apostle Peter mentions him as an example of a false messiah. The apostle refers to him to show that the messianic movements arising in his own time are not new: Theudas is an ancient example. His mention serves to reassure the disciples: false christs and false prophets arise, but their cause always perishes.
G2333.portee: Theudas embodies in the early Church the danger of false messiahs and false religious promises. His example helps early Christians discern true from false: a leader who claims to be sent by God but whose movement collapses immediately reveals his imposture. This reinforces faith in Jesus, the true Messiah, whose kingdom will never perish.

sens: Look attentively, observe
Contemplate with admiration or interest
Attend an event, be a witness
Perceive, notice, discern
Experience, know through experience
G2334.detail: 1. Look attentively, observe: this means to fix one's attention on something or someone to examine it. The women at the foot of the cross "looked" at Jesus from a distance (Matthew 27:55): they kept their eyes fixed on him in this grave moment. 2. Contemplate with admiration or interest: to observe something remarkable, often with fascination. The crowd "saw" the miracles of Jesus (John 6:2): they were captivated by his works of power. 3. Attend an event, be a witness: to be present and watch what is happening. The angels ask Mary to "come see" where the Lord had been laid (John 20:12), inviting her to verify the resurrection with her own eyes. 4. Perceive, notice, discern: to grasp with the eyes or mind what exists. Jesus says, "I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning" (Luke 10:18): he clearly perceives this spiritual reality. 5. Experience, know through experience: to undergo or live through an event. "Whoever believes in me will never see death" (John 8:51) means that they will never experience eternal death.
G2334.origine: The word comes from the Greek θεωρός (theoros), which designates a spectator, an attentive observer. The same root appears in "theater": it is the place where one looks. The word evokes the idea of fixing one's gaze on something with intention. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates רָאָה (see) and חָזָה (contemplate), both of which mean to perceive by sight.
G2334.emploi: This verb appears about 56 times in the New Testament, especially in John and in Acts. It first denotes the simple action of looking (Matthew 27:55, Mark 15:40), then expands to the attentive observation of remarkable facts, particularly the miracles of Jesus (John 6:2, 2:23). In John, particularly, "see" takes on a spiritual depth: "whoever sees me sees the one who sent me" (John 12:45) means perceiving the unity of the Father and the Son. In Acts, the word describes the apostles who observe the wonders and signs (Acts 4:13, 8:13). In a few passages (John 8:51, 17:24), it acquires the meaning of "experience" or "know through experience." Jesus also uses the verb to express his own supernatural vision: he "saw" Satan fall from heaven (Luke 10:18).
G2334.portee: For the believer, this word invites us to truly "see" Jesus and his works, not in a passive or distracted manner, but with attention and faith. This is particularly important in John: seeing the works of Jesus is an invitation to recognize who he truly is.
