When Jesus says, "whoever sees me sees the Father," he calls for a deep spiritual vision, not limited to mere external observation. This verb also reminds us that the Christian faith is not abstract: it involves the living contemplation of what God does and reveals.

sens: act of seeing, fact of attending an event
what is offered to the view, scene, remarkable event
G2335.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the act of looking, being a witness to something. It is the act of seeing together, attending a public event. In Luke 23:48, it is the crowd gathered to witness the spectacle of Christ's crucifixion. 2. By extension, it designates what one sees: a scene, a remarkable event, particularly when it strikes the mind. At the cross, this spectacle is the death of Jesus — an event so striking that the witnesses return, beating their breasts, deeply troubled.
G2335.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb théōréō ("to see," "to look," "to contemplate"). It belongs to the family of words related to vision and attentive observation. The root would first evoke the idea of "looking" or "observing," as one looks at a spectacle in a theater. This word has retained this sense of active vision, of conscious observation of an event.
G2335.emploi: The word appears only once in the Gospels in French, in Luke 23:48. It designates the scene of the cross seen by the crowd: not simply an event, but the fact that a multitude observes it and witnesses it. What makes this moment a "theôria" is that it is public, visible, imbued with a certain solemnity. The spectators are shaken: they see not just an act, but a revelation.
G2335.portee: This word reminds us that the death of Christ is not a hidden or private event, but public and visible. The crowd "witnesses" the cross; they are witnesses. For the Christian, this spectacle — the crucifixion — remains the heart of the Gospel: it is what we look at, what we contemplate, to understand the heart of God. Being a Christian is, in a sense, becoming a spectator of this spectacle and allowing it to transform one's heart.

sens: Case that envelops the blade of a sword or saber
Container or box intended to store, preserve something
G2336.detail: 1. The sheath is the case made of leather, wood, or metal that slides over the blade of a sword to protect it and keep it still when not in use. Jesus uses this concrete word when he says to Peter: "Put your sword into the sheath" (John 18:11), commanding him to put away his weapon at the moment of his arrest. 2. In a broader sense, the word designates any container or box used to store, preserve, or transport objects, like a box or protective case, by analogy with the sheath of the sword.
G2336.origine: The Greek word "thēkē" comes from the verb "tithēmi" ("to place, to put, to set"): it is literally a place where something is put to be preserved. The same root has produced other Greek words related to preservation or deposit. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "bayit" ("house") in Exodus 25:27, showing how the idea of "container" or "receptacle" is fundamental to the word.
G2336.emploi: The word "sheath" appears only once in the New Testament, in John 18:11. Jesus uses it in a dramatic context: at the moment of his arrest, Peter drew the sword to defend his master, but Jesus rebukes him by commanding him to put his sword into the sheath. This detail emphasizes Jesus' refusal to resort to armed violence and his voluntary acceptance of the passion. The word remains very concrete and does not take on a figurative meaning in biblical usage.
G2336.portee: This passage reminds the disciples and readers that the kingdom of Jesus is not a kingdom of armed force. By ordering Peter to sheath his sword, Jesus teaches that trust in God and obedience to the Father are superior to legitimate defense or resorting to weapons. This simple gesture — putting away a sword — thus becomes a symbol of renouncing violence and submitting to God's salvific plan.

sens: To hunt an animal to capture it
To set a trap for someone to capture or harm them
Figuratively: to seek to catch someone off guard in their words or actions
G2340.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of hunting: pursuing an animal to capture or kill it. This is the basic image of the Greek word.

2. It then shifts to the idea of setting a trap, net, or snare for a beast, thus capturing it by cunning rather than by pursuit.

3. Figuratively, it means to seek to catch someone off guard, to corner them in a clumsy word or reprehensible act. In Luke 11:54, Jesus' enemies "were lying in wait for Him, to catch something out of His mouth": they hoped to make Him say something they could use against Him.
G2340.origine: The word comes from the root θήρα (thēra), which means "hunting" or "game." The same family is found in θήρ (thēr), "wild beast" or "animal." The image is that of the hunter on the lookout: he observes his prey, prepares his trap, then springs or captures it. In Hebrew, this verb corresponds to צוּד (tsûd), which also carries the idea of capturing or trapping.
G2340.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:54. Jesus denounces the scribes and Pharisees who crowded around Him to "surprise" Him — that is, to set verbal traps in hopes of catching Him off guard. The context shows that it is a hunt for words: these adversaries were watching every word Jesus spoke, ready to twist it into an accusation. The verb thus emphasizes the premeditation and malice of this pursuit.
G2340.portee: This verse exposes the tactic of those who reject Jesus: rather than sincerely seeking the truth, they spy, they watch, they set traps. The word invites us to examine our own intentions when we listen to a word or teaching: are we hunting for faults or seeking the good? It also calls us to vigilance: the disciple of Jesus must know that malice lurks and hides under the guise of innocent questions.

sens: To face wild animals in an arena or combat place
Figuratively, to confront fierce and dangerous enemies or adversaries
G2341.detail:
1. Literally, this verb describes the fight against wild beasts, as practiced in Roman arenas where gladiators and condemned individuals had to face lions, bears, or other ferocious animals to entertain the crowd. It is an extreme trial that puts life in danger.

2. Figuratively, Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 15:32 to describe his spiritual battles and persecutions in Ephesus: "If, from a human point of view, I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus." He speaks not of real animals, but of hostile forces, fierce and cruel adversaries who oppose him. It is a poetic image to express the intensity and violence of the struggle he faced.
G2341.origine: The Greek word combines θηρίον (thérion, "wild beast") and μάχομαι (machomaï, "to fight"). This composition literally describes the fight against fierce animals, a reality of the ancient Roman world where such combats were spectacular and deadly. Paul borrows this familiar image for his readers to express the intensity of his spiritual battle.
G2341.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:32. Paul uses it in his argument about the resurrection of the dead: he questions the meaning of his sufferings and commitment if the resurrection does not exist. The expression "fighting against wild beasts" symbolically summarizes all the trials he endured for the Gospel, particularly in Ephesus where he faced strong opposition. It is a rhetorical way to emphasize the extreme nature of his sacrifice.
G2341.portee: This image reminds the reader that the Christian life is not an easy path, but a real battle against hostile forces. For Paul, this fight only makes sense if the resurrection is true; otherwise, all sacrifice is in vain. This invites the believer to reflect on the foundation of their commitment: is it for an eternal hope or for fleeting earthly advantages?

sens: wild animal
any living creature
hostile and tyrannical power figuratively represented by an animal
G2342.detail:
1. The word primarily designates wild animals, as opposed to domesticated animals or humans. In Mark 1:13, Jesus is "with the wild beasts" during His time in the wilderness, and in James 3:7, "all kinds of beasts and birds" are enumerated.
2. It can refer to any animal or living creature, domesticated or not. In Acts 10:12 and 11:6, the vision contains various "beasts," birds, and reptiles, without distinction between wild and tame.
3. In Revelation, the word takes on a figurative meaning to designate evil powers: the "beast" of Revelation 13:4 is the Antichrist or the empire hostile to God, worshiped as a formidable power. The same term applies to this monstrous creature that comes from the sea in Revelation 13:1-2 and to all its manifestations.
4. By extension, it symbolizes everything that is brutal, irrational, or contrary to God: a beast is devoid of reason and can only obey its instinct for destruction.
G2342.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient root that evokes hunting and wild animals. It is a diminutive of θήρ (thēr), which literally means "ferocious beast." It translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew word חַיָּה (chaya), which designates any living animal, particularly wild beasts. The Greek form has gained a nuance: it can designate both a small animal and an impressive creature.
G2342.emploi: The word appears 39 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels and epistles, it mostly retains its literal meaning: the wild animals of the desert (Mark 1:13), the creatures of Peter's vision (Acts 10:12 and 11:6), the snakes that bit Paul (Acts 28:4-5). But Revelation completely transforms its usage: the "beast" becomes a figure of anti-divine and tyrannical power, appearing dozens of times to designate the persecuting empire worshiped by those who abandon God. This same "beast" manifests in various forms: the one that rises from the sea (Revelation 13:1), the one with seven heads (Revelation 13:2-3), the one that speaks blasphemies (Revelation 13:11). The beast receives the worship of the world (Revelation 13:4, 15), and its number is 666 (Revelation 13:18).
G2342.portee: Understanding the word "beast" in the Bible invites the reader to two reflections. First, it reminds us that God created and accepts wild animals: in Mark 1:13, Jesus shares the wilderness with them, establishing a primitive peace. Second, the apocalyptic usage warns the believer: the earthly powers that persecute and demand worship are merely "beasts," devoid of true wisdom and destined for ultimate defeat. It is an invitation not to fear tyrannical power, but to place one's trust in God alone.

sens: To accumulate material wealth by keeping it for oneself
To gradually set aside a sum of money or goods
Figuratively: to accumulate, to build up a reserve of abstract things (anger, judgment)
G2343.detail:
1. The most common meaning is to accumulate wealth by hoarding it jealously. Jesus warns against those who "store up treasures on earth" (Matthew 6:19) — the image is that of a reserve kept, piled up at home, but which is fragile and perishable. This is also the case of the rich man who "stores up treasures for himself" (Luke 12:21) without caring for God: he fills his vault, but his soul remains empty.
2. The word also refers to the action of gradually setting aside, saving. Saint Paul asks the Corinthians to "set aside" an offering each week according to their means (1 Corinthians 16:2) — it is a reserve built up slowly, voluntarily. Parents "accumulate" for their children (2 Corinthians 12:14), meaning they save and economize over time.
3. Figuratively, the word describes the accumulation of spiritual or moral realities. The hard-hearted man "stores up wrath" (Romans 2:5) — as if, by refusing to repent, he piles up divine anger day after day, preparing for himself an ever heavier judgment. It is the image of a moral debt that accumulates.
G2343.origine: The word comes from the Greek thésauros, which literally means "treasure" or "chest." The verb thésaurizô adds the idea of action: to put into the treasure, to constitute a treasure. The basic image is therefore that of a reserve that is hidden, that is protected — just as one hides a treasure safely. The corresponding Hebrew root often translated by this word is tzáphan, which means "to hide, to put in secret." The same Greek verb is also used for abstract realities: one can "accumulate" anger, judgment, just as one accumulates gold.
G2343.emploi: The word appears about 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. In Matthew, Jesus uses it twice (6:19-20) to contrast the accumulation of earthly riches with that of heavenly treasures — it is a call to a change of priorities. In Luke and Paul, the word takes on a broader meaning: it can refer to honest saving (1 Corinthians 16:2, 2 Corinthians 12:14), but also to the culpable accumulation of divine judgment by refusing to repent (Romans 2:5). The nuance therefore varies: the word is not condemnable in itself, but Jesus denounces the one who "accumulates" without consideration for God or others.
G2343.portee: This word invites us to examine our priorities: on what do we place our efforts and hopes? Are we accumulating wealth that will escape us at death, or "treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:20) — that is, a life of faith, generosity, and righteousness? It also shows us a truth often hidden: our moral choices accumulate. Each refusal to repent, each hardening of the heart "stores up" judgment. It is a call to vigilance: what we "set aside" today, spiritually speaking, we will carry tomorrow.

sens: chest, box, or container holding precious items
reserve, repository, a place where wealth is accumulated and kept
precious goods, accumulated value, wealth
that which is precious to the heart and soul, what one truly cherishes
wisdom and knowledge of God in Jesus Christ
G2344.detail:
1. The treasure in the concrete sense first: it is a chest, a box where valuable things are stored. In Matthew 2:11, the wise men "opened their treasures" — these were portable boxes from which they took gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
2. It is also a storage place, a reserve: a treasurer, a householder who "brings out of his treasure things new and old" (Matthew 13:52) draws from what he has accumulated and preserved.
3. The word then designates the wealth itself, the precious goods. Jesus speaks of "storing up treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:20) — it refers to values, lasting spiritual riches.
4. Jesus goes further: the treasure is what comes from the depths of the heart, what fills it. "A good man brings out good things from his good treasure" (Matthew 12:35) — the heart is a reservoir, filled with what one has truly put into it.
5. Finally, in Colossians 2:3, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are "hidden in Christ Jesus" — Jesus himself is the true wealth, the inexhaustible reserve of what gives life.
G2344.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to place, to put." A treasure is what has been set aside, preserved, kept precious. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew word "ôtzar" (אוֹצָר), which has the same meaning: a storehouse, a warehouse, a chest of riches. Wealthy ancient families kept their precious goods in such locked boxes.
G2344.emploi: The word "treasure" appears 16 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew and Luke. There are first the concrete uses: the boxes of the wise men (Matthew 2:11), the storages of the Temple or the house (Matthew 13:52). But Jesus constantly spiritualizes it. In Matthew 6:19-21, he contrasts earthly treasures — eaten away by moth and rust, taken by thieves — with heavenly treasures, lasting and secure. He links treasure to inner life in Matthew 12:35 and Luke 6:45: the treasure of the heart is what truly flows from it. In Paul (2 Corinthians 4:7, Colossians 2:3), Christ is the treasure in which all the riches of God are hidden.
G2344.portee: This word invites the Christian to discern their true riches: not what corrupts or is lost, but what endures in Christ Jesus. It highlights that the heart reveals its treasures through its actions and words — one becomes what one cherishes. The accumulation of earthly riches diverts from the true, while "storing up treasures in heaven" — through faith, obedience, generosity — fills the soul with an indestructible wealth. It is a call to reorient one's desires toward what lasts.

sens: To make physical contact with something or someone
To harm, injure, or affect negatively
G2345.detail:
1. Touch means to make physical contact with something — to bring it into contact with one's hand or body. This is the simplest and most concrete meaning. In Colossians 2:21, the Apostle Paul cites ascetic rules that forbid touching certain things: "Do not handle! Do not taste! Do not touch!" The image is that of direct contact with an object. In Hebrews 12:20, it speaks of a beast that would touch the mountain — again, this is a material contact that would render the mountain impure according to the law of Moses.

2. Touch can also mean "to harm," "to reach" someone in the sense of causing them injury or affecting them negatively. This is a more figurative extension of physical contact: when one touches someone to harm them, they reach them. In Hebrews 11:28, it refers to the destroyer who was not to touch the firstborn of the Israelites — meaning to strike them, to put them to death. The Greek word touches here on the meaning of the Hebrew נָגַע (nâga'), which carries this dual nuance.
G2345.origine: The verb θιγγάνω comes from a Greek root that expresses the idea of contact or reach. In ancient Greek, it often translates the Hebrew נָגַע (nâga'), a verb from the family of "plague" or "blow." This Hebrew root primarily denotes physical contact, and by extension, being affected, touched by a disease, a plague, or a threat. The Greek verb encompasses this range of meanings: from simple contact to harmful reach.
G2345.emploi: The verb θιγγάνω appears three times in the New Testament, always in the later part (Paul's epistles and the epistle to the Hebrews). In Colossians 2:21, it denotes the act of touching in a material and literal sense, in a context of ascetic prescriptions. In Hebrews 11:28 and 12:20, both of which cite or refer back to the Mosaic law, the verb takes on a darker hue: to touch means "to harm," "to attack." It is the same verb that encompasses two registers — neutral contact and threat — depending on the context. The connection with the Hebrew נָגַע confirms this dual value in biblical thought.
G2345.portee: This word helps us see how the Bible speaks of what separates us from God. In Colossians 2:21, Paul warns against human rules that claim to keep evil at bay through abstention and ritual prohibition. In Hebrews 11:28 and 12:20, the word evokes divine protection: God prevents the destroyer from touching the Israelites through the Passover, just as no one could touch the mountain of Sinai without perishing. It is a reminder that our security comes not from our efforts to keep ourselves at a distance, but from God's grace and protection.

sens: To compress, physically press
To narrow, make tight
To oppress, overwhelm someone with difficulties
To torment, cause suffering
To experience distress or suffering
G2346.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to press, compress, like a crowd pressing against someone. Mark 3:9 shows this: Jesus fears being "pressed" by the multitude surrounding Him and wants to escape by boat.

2. From a concrete sense to space: a road can be "narrowed" or tight, meaning compressed on all sides. Matthew 7:14 speaks of the "narrow way" that leads to life — a difficult, tight path, with no room to stray.

3. The major sense is figurative: to afflict someone, to oppress them, to weigh them down with trials. Paul uses this word to describe the sufferings he endures: in 2 Corinthians 1:6, he says "we are afflicted" by tribulations, but this serves to comfort other Christians.

4. It is also to torment from within, to cause moral and spiritual suffering. Persecution, fear, temptations, trials — all of this "afflicts" the believer and presses from all sides.

5. Passive: to be afflicted means to endure distress. In 2 Corinthians 4:8, Paul lists his misfortunes: "we are pressed on every side, but not crushed" — an image of a life compressed by difficulties, but not crushed.
G2346.origine: The Greek verb comes from a root that means "to squeeze, compress." Its primary image is physical: it is the act of pressing or crushing something between two forces. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it generally translates the Hebrew word צוּר (tsûr), which has the same meaning: to squeeze, confine, besiege. The word has naturally shifted towards the figurative sense of tormenting, afflicting, overwhelming — as if misfortunes close in on a person's vital space. Compound words with the same root (sunthLibō, apothLibō) share this idea.
G2346.emploi: The verb θλίβω (afflict) appears about 10 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. In the Gospels, it remains close to the concrete: physically pressing (Mark 3:9) or describing a narrow road (Matthew 7:14). In Paul, the meaning becomes almost technical to designate the tribulations, persecutions, sufferings that a Christian endures. In 2 Corinthians (1:6, 4:8, 7:5), Paul uses the passive form ("to be afflicted") to list his own misfortunes — imprisonment, beatings, fatigue — with a tone that mixes real suffering and assurance in God. In 1 Thessalonians 3:4 and 2 Thessalonians 1:6-7, the word is linked to the tribulations that believers will face before the final judgment. Hebrews 11:37 cites the saints of the Old Testament who were "afflicted" — tortured, stoned, exiled. The word always oscillates between physical pressure and the spiritual weight of trial.
G2346.portee: This word reminds the believer that suffering is a biblical reality, not an accident or a hidden curse. It can come from the outside (persecution, crowd, danger) or from within (fear, moral distress). But the Bible never isolates affliction from God's consolation: Paul, "afflicted" by tribulations, draws comfort for others (2 Corinthians 1:6). This invites us to see trials not as proof of God's absence, but as a narrow yet true path, a necessary passage for those who follow Christ. It is also an invitation to empathize with those who suffer, just as the saints of the Old Testament suffered before the promise.

sens: Physical pressure, oppression
Intense emotional suffering, distress of the heart
Trial that tests faith
Persecution because of Christian faith
Time of eschatological trials before the end of times
G2347.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical pressure, an oppression that crushes: this is the original image. However, in the Bible, it is rarely used in a purely material sense.
2. It mainly signifies intense moral suffering, a distress of the heart that overwhelms the one who endures it. Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 2:4 that he wrote "in great affliction, with an anguished heart."
3. The word designates the trial that comes to test and prove the believer's faith: in Matthew 13:21, when "tribulation" arises because of the word, it reveals whether the faith has deep roots.
4. It often takes on the meaning of persecution against Christians for their faith: in Matthew 24:9 and Mark 13:19, Jesus speaks of the "tribulations" that will come upon his disciples.
5. In Revelation and Jesus' discourses, the word refers to the great trials of the end times, the calamities that accompany the approach of the end of the world (Matthew 24:21, Revelation 7:14).
G2347.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to press, to compress." Its basic image is that of a crushing pressure, a suffocating embrace. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates the word צָרָה (tsarah), which means narrowness, anguish, distress: the idea is that one is squeezed on all sides, with no way out. The word has retained in the Greek Bible and the New Testament its meaning of a trial that crushes and compresses the believer's soul.
G2347.emploi: The word is very frequent in the New Testament (42 occurrences), especially in Paul's epistles and in Revelation. It designates the trials that Christians encounter: personal suffering (John 16:21 speaks of the suffering of childbirth), moral affliction (2 Corinthians 2:4), persecution for faith (Matthew 13:21, Mark 4:17). Paul constantly returns to it to exhort believers to perseverance and joy even in tribulation (Romans 12:12: "rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation"). In the eschatological passages of Jesus (Matthew 24, Mark 13), it designates the great tribulations of the end times. Revelation speaks of the saints who come out of the "great tribulation" (7:14), sanctified by the trials.
G2347.portee: The word reminds Christians that suffering and trial are normal in the life of faith, not anomalies. Jesus promises tribulations to his disciples, but also peace in him and final victory. Understanding this word helps the believer to see their trials not as arbitrary punishments, but as the necessary passage of sanctification and growth in Christ. It is a call to patience, trust, and to remember that even in tribulation, God is faithful.

sens: Cease to live, leave life
Be in a state of death
Perish, succumb
Be spiritually inert, without true life
G2348.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning: to pass from life to death, to breathe one's last. This is physical death, the complete cessation of life in the body. Jesus speaks of this in Matthew 2:20 when the angel warns Joseph that "those who sought the child's life are dead," meaning that Herod and his assassins have disappeared.
2. To be dead: to remain in the state of death, the past participle of the verb "to die." Pilate "was amazed that he was dead so soon" (Mark 15:44), astonishment at the present state of Jesus' body. This also refers to the lifeless body: in Luke 7:12, "they were carrying out a dead man," a corpse being taken to the grave.
3. To die violently, to perish: when Paul is stoned in Lystra, his enemies leave him "thinking he was dead" (Acts 14:19). This refers to violent, tragic death.
4. To die spiritually, to be spiritually inert: in 1 Timothy 5:6, Paul says that a widow who delights in luxury and idleness "is dead" even though she is still physically alive. This is a death of the soul, a spiritual incapacity, the absence of true life with God.
G2348.origine: The Greek θνήσκω comes from a root that simply evokes the act of ceasing to live, the extinction of life. This verb is the common translation of the Hebrew word מוּת (to die) in the ancient Greek Scriptures. The Greeks used this verb to describe the universal and fatal event: to die.
G2348.emploi: The verb appears eleven times in the New Testament, almost always to describe physical death. It is mostly found in the Gospels, particularly around the death of Jesus (Mark 15:44, John 19:33) and the resurrections he performs (Luke 7:12, John 11:44). In Acts, it refers to the violent death of Paul being stoned (14:19). A remarkable occurrence is found in 1 Timothy 5:6, where Paul uses it figuratively: a widow given to luxury "is dead" spiritually, though alive in appearance. This shift from the literal to the figurative shows how the Bible uses the image of physical death to express the death of the soul.
G2348.portee: This word reminds us of one of the gravest realities of sin: death is the final enemy, the wages of sin. It also confronts us with the power of Jesus: he alone conquers and transcends death. Finally, the passage from 1 Timothy invites the Christian to ask whether they are truly living or allowing themselves to die spiritually — a question of true life in Christ.

sens: Subject to death, capable of dying
Belonging to the human condition marked by death
Destined to disappear, not to last eternally
G2349.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what is subject to death, what cannot escape death — this is the very condition of every human being. In Romans 8:11, Paul speaks of "your mortal bodies" that God will give life to: he refers to the physical body as we have it now, fragile and perishable.
2. By extension, the word characterizes everything that participates in human fragility and impermanence. In 1 Corinthians 15:53-54, Paul contrasts the "mortal" body (which dies, which decays) with the "immortal" body (which does not die anymore): here, "mortal" describes our current, temporal condition, contrasted with the promised resurrection.
3. The word can also qualify what is destined for death or decline — not only the body, but what envelops it: in 2 Corinthians 5:4, Paul speaks of "what is mortal" being swallowed up by life, referring to our present human nature as it must be transformed.
G2349.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb θνήσκω (to die) and literally means "subject to death." The root expresses the idea of death, of mortality that strikes every living being. In ancient Greek, it is the natural adjective to say that a creature is not immortal, that it shares the mortal condition. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate Hebrew words describing death and the fragility of man.
G2349.emploi: The word appears only six times in the New Testament, all in Paul's epistles. It mainly recurs in 1 Corinthians 15 and 2 Corinthians 4-5, passages where Paul discusses resurrection and transformation of the body: it is the contrast between what dies and what will live forever that gives the word all its strength. In Romans 6:12 and 8:11, it refers to the fleshly body over which sin reigns or which the Spirit gives life. The context is always theological: Paul is not simply speaking of a biological reality, but of a spiritual condition and a promise of transformation.
G2349.portee: This word reminds the Christian of their current fragility and their hope for resurrection. It is not meant to depress, but to place hope in the right place: our mortal body is not our end. At the same time, it invites us not to enslave this mortal body to sin (Romans 6:12), since it is called to live eternally in Christ. It is a word of veiled hope: we recognize what we are, in order to better desire what we will be.

sens: Emit loud and confusing sounds, clamor
Express emotion loudly, especially by lamenting
Disturb order, throw someone into confusion
G2350.detail:
1. The word primarily describes an intense and confusing noise. In Matthew 9:23, Jesus enters the house of the ruler and finds a "noisy" crowd of flute players and mourners; in Mark 5:39, Jesus tells the people who are "making noise" to be quiet, as they disturb the solemn moment.
2. It then denotes emotional clamor: ostentatious lamentation, groans, and cries expressed without restraint. This agitation of the heart manifests itself through noise and disorder. Luke 10:41 uses it to describe Martha's inner turmoil, who is "worried" under the weight of her concerns.
3. In the most figurative sense, the verb means to disturb, to throw into confusion and disruption. In Acts 17:5, jealous Jews cause "agitation" in the city by spreading false accusations and disorder. In Acts 20:10, Paul tells the "troubled" disciples not to be downcast over the death of young Eutychus.
G2350.origine: The word comes from the noun θόρυβος (thorubos), "tumult, noise." It is the image of noise that stirs and troubles: a sound chaos that paralyzes or confuses. The verb θορυβέω literally means "to produce thorubos." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew roots evoking tumult, agitation, or panic.
G2350.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily describes the clamor of mourners and musicians at Jewish funerals: it is a conventional, expected noise in mourning. Jesus opposes it, as in Matthew 9:23 and Mark 5:39, indicating that this emotional tumult is misplaced in His presence. In Luke 10:41, the same verb characterizes Martha's emotional agitation—not noise in the strict sense, but the worry that torments her. In Acts, the meaning becomes political and social: the agitation that one "provokes" or spreads is that of civic disorder, an excited crowd, riots. The word thus transitions from auditory clamor to heart agitation, then to public disorder.
G2350.portee: Understanding this verb helps the believer grasp how Jesus and the apostles respond to emotional noise: neither appearance nor the tumult of mourning or anxiety should divert us from trust in God. Martha is troubled by many things, but Jesus calls her to peace. And in the face of civic troubles and accusations, Paul exhorts tranquility, assuring that God is in control of the situation.

sens: Confused and deafening noise
Agitation of an excited or disorderly crowd
Commotion, public disturbance
G2351.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes an intense and confusing noise, that made by a multitude of voices speaking, shouting, or weeping at the same time. At the house of the synagogue ruler, Jesus encounters a "noisy" crowd of people who are weeping and crying out loudly (Mark 5:38): this is the characteristic noise of collective emotion. 2. It especially refers to the agitation of an excited crowd—people gathered en masse and disturbed. The chief priests fear to arrest Jesus during the feast, lest there be a "tumult" among the people (Matthew 26:5; Mark 14:2): they dread an explosion from the crowd. 3. It also signifies a public disturbance, a civil commotion: in Jerusalem, such a noise from the crowd arises during the sedition against Paul that a centurion must take him to the fortress for safety, as the "tumult" prevents any order (Acts 21:34).
G2351.origine: The Greek word thorubos literally denotes a noise, a sound agitation. It comes from the same family as the verb thorubéô ("to make noise, to disturb"). The Old Testament uses similar words, notably hâmôn, which depicts the buzzing of a crowd or an army. It is a word that paints through sound: it evokes less the abstract idea of disorder than the sensory experience of auditory chaos and the agitation that one hears and feels.
G2351.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew (2 times) and Mark (2 times), and in Acts (3 times). It always describes a troubled crowd situation. In Matthew and Mark, it is the fear of a tumult that drives the authorities to avoid a public arrest of Jesus. In Luke (Acts), the tumult is real: the riot in Ephesus (Acts 20:1), the confusion in Jerusalem surrounding Paul (Acts 21:34, 24:18). The word paints each time the atmosphere of a passionate crowd, uncontrollable by its very mass.
G2351.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power of the crowd and its unpredictability. It shows that the Gospel and the apostolic testimony arise in a context of strong collective emotions, often hostile. For the believer, it is a lesson: do not be swept away by the passion of the multitude, but remain anchored in the truth of Christ, which no tumult can shake.

sens: Reduce to pieces, shatter
Weaken, bring down (figurative)
G2352.detail:
1. To break means to reduce something to pieces, to shatter it. This is the physical and concrete sense of the word: to break what is whole. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it in Deuteronomy 28:33 and Isaiah 42:4 to describe things that are broken into pieces.
2. Figuratively, to break means to weaken, to bring down, to break someone's heart or spirit. In Luke 4:18, Jesus quotes Isaiah 58:6: He comes "to break the chains of the captives," which means to free the oppressed by breaking their bonds, but also figuratively to uplift those whose spirits are crushed.
G2352.origine: The verb θραύω comes from a root that evokes the idea of striking and breaking. In Hebrew, the word it often translates is שׁבר (shavar), which has the same range of meanings: to break, to shatter, to crush, but also to reduce to nothing or to humiliate. This root expresses the violent action of destroying the integrity of something.
G2352.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:18, where Jesus reads the passage from the prophet Isaiah in the synagogue of Nazareth. He declares that the Spirit of the Lord has anointed Him "to break the chains of the captives." The context is that of the liberation of the oppressed and the proclamation of good news. The word evokes both the physical breaking of chains and, in a broader sense, the spiritual liberation and uplifting of broken hearts.
G2352.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that Jesus comes not only to break the visible chains of oppression but also to free from everything that imprisons: guilt, shame, despair. It invites us to see in Jesus the Liberator who breaks what crushes us and restores us to freedom.

sens: A group of domesticated animals raised together
Livestock, particularly pack or draft animals
G2353.detail:
1. The word designates a group of animals that are fed and raised together. It is the image of the shepherd who watches over his flock, keeps them safe, and leads them to pasture. In John 4:12, Jesus asks the Samaritan woman: "Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?" — the flock here is a precious asset, a wealth inherited from generation to generation.
2. The word can also more broadly refer to livestock, the totality of farm or grazing animals one possesses. It is a concrete, measurable wealth that requires care and work.
G2353.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to feed," "to raise." It originally designates what has been fed, what is raised — hence "nursling" or "young raised." When applied to animals, it takes on the specific meaning of "livestock that is fed." It is a common word in ancient Greek literature to talk about flocks and husbandry.
G2353.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 4:12. It refers to Jacob's material wealth — in biblical times, owning a large flock was a sign of prosperity and blessing. Jesus uses it to show that in spiritual matters, a personal encounter with the Messiah far surpasses the inheritances of the past, even that of a founding patriarch.
G2353.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not despise material goods — Jacob received a well, a flock, a family — but it places these riches in their proper context. The Lord Jesus invites us to seek first the living water, the gift of God that quenches eternal thirst, far beyond what ancestors may have bequeathed. For the believer, it is an invitation to evaluate what truly matters.

sens: To express pain or sorrow through complaints and cries
To sing or recite plaintive words, notably a lament or a funeral song
To express regret or desolation in the face of an unfortunate event
G2354.detail:
1. To lament is to express one's pain, sorrow, or affliction loudly. It is to weep, to cry out one's sadness. In Luke 23:27, the women "lamented" over Jesus as they followed him to the cross, beating their breasts in a sign of deep sorrow.

2. The word also refers to the act of singing or reciting plaintive words, laments, especially funeral songs. In Matthew 11:17 and Luke 7:32, people "sing laments" as one would play sad music — it is a concerted act, a recognized form of expression of mourning.

3. More broadly, to lament is to manifest one's desolation, regret, or concern in the face of misfortune. In John 16:20, the disciples "will lament" because Jesus is leaving, thus expressing their sadness and distress over this separation.
G2354.origine: The word comes from the noun θρῆνος (thrênos), which means "lament," "funeral song," or "complaint." It shares the same root as words expressing ritual lamentation, which was a common practice in the ancient world. The verb describes the action of producing this lament, whether spontaneous or ritualized.
G2354.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, primarily in Luke and the Gospel of John. It is first used to describe the singing of a lament, a musical practice associated with sadness or mourning (Matthew 11:17, Luke 7:32). It is also used for the act of weeping and complaining directly about someone or something (Luke 23:27: the women lament over Jesus). Finally, John 16:20 uses it to express the emotional pain of the disciples at Jesus' departure. The context varies from ritual or musical mourning to personal expressions of grief.
G2354.portee: This verb helps the reader understand the intensity of emotions — joy and sadness, mourning and comfort — in spiritual life. The women lamenting over Jesus (Luke 23:27) show how humanity felt the weight of his death, while John 16:20 teaches that the disciples' sorrow will be turned into joy: lamentation is not the final word for those who believe in the risen Christ.

sens: A cry of pain and sadness expressed in the face of a loss or death
A loud expression of grief through weeping and wailing
The act of weeping over someone or something that is lost
G2355.detail:
1. A lamentation is a cry of pain uttered in the face of death or an irreparable loss. It is more than a simple tear: it is the audible and complete expression of sadness, often collective, as when mourning a dead person or a lost child. In Matthew 2:18, Herod ordered the massacre of the children of Bethlehem, and in Rama, one hears "weeping and great lamentation": Rachel, the ancestral mother of the northern tribes, weeps for her lost children and refuses to be comforted.
2. This word particularly designates the cries and wailings that accompany mourning — lamentation is the language of unrestrained grief. Rachel cannot accept the death of her children: she refuses consolation because the loss is definitive. It is a cry that says, "my child will never return."
3. Lamentation also evokes the idea of mourning: one weeps over something or someone that is past. The word carries the image of women or a community expressing their pain aloud, without shame, in the face of the irreparable.
G2355.origine: The Greek word θρῆνος comes from a root related to crying and wailing. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew word קִינָה (qinah), which designates funeral lamentation or mourning song — a poetic genre of the ancient East that was highly developed in Israel. The same root gives the verb "to weep" or "to lament," and the noun designates the act of weeping collectively, often with a ritual or poetic dimension.
G2355.emploi: The word appears only once in Matthew 2:18, in the account of the massacre of the innocents. Matthew cites Jeremiah 31:15, a prophetic oracle about Rachel weeping for her children in exile. By reporting Herod's massacre, Matthew sees this ancient word fulfilled: lamentations are the sign of irreparable suffering. The context is one of mourning and refusal of consolation — Rachel cannot accept the death of her children because this death is definitive. It is a moment of absolute sadness, expressed through crying and lamentation.
G2355.portee: Lamentation reminds us that the Bible does not ask the believer to repress their pain in the face of death. Rachel weeps, and that is right. But this passage also teaches that even in the deepest despair, God does not abandon his people: he sees the tears and laments of those who suffer. For the Christian, this image of Rachel weeping for her children is illuminated by the light of resurrection in Christ: there is hope beyond lamentation.

sens: External practice of faith, worship and observances
Set of rites and devotions addressed to a deity
Devotion to superhuman powers (angels, spirits)
Religious attitude or professed belief
G2356.detail:
1. "Religion" is primarily the external and visible practice of worship: it is what is seen, what is done publicly. Paul says he lived according to the Pharisaic sect "the most rigid of our religion" (Acts 26:5), referring to the strict observance of laws and traditions. It is the visible side, the gestures and the rules.

2. Religion is also a worship directed towards a superhuman power. In Colossians 2:18, it speaks of the "worship of angels" — a particular devotion, a form of adoration given to these celestial beings. It is a religious manifestation directed towards a deity.

3. But James goes further: a religion can be formal and vain (James 1:26). One who does not control their tongue "deceives their heart," and their religion is empty — it is a warning against religious hypocrisy, when one displays piety without living it.

4. Conversely, "pure religion" (James 1:27) is not just rites; it consists of visiting orphans and widows, serving the unfortunate. It is a religion that translates into concrete acts of charity and separation from evil.
G2356.origine: The word comes from the adjective thrêskos ("religious," "pious"), which evokes the attitude of one who fears a deity and respects its worship. Religion is thus the cultic practice born of this respectful fear. It is a Greek word that speaks, without a clear Indo-European root, emphasizing the external and ceremonial aspect much more than the inner conviction.
G2356.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Paul or James. In Acts 26:5, Paul describes himself as an orthodox Pharisee, attached to a certain religious form. In Colossians 2:18, it is a warning against a false religion, one that worships angels. In James, the word is crucial: first in 1:26, formal religion that is displayed in words but not in deeds; then in 1:27, true religion that is proven by helping the poor and moral purity. James shows that true religion is not limited to appearances.
G2356.portee: This word challenges believers to distinguish between facade religion and true faith that transforms life. For those who listen to James, there is no refuge in rites and pious words: the religion worthy of the name must produce charity, humility, and holiness. It is a call to spiritual authenticity, not to deceive oneself under the guise of piety.

sens: Who scrupulously observes the external practices of divine worship
Who shows zeal for the forms of religion
G2357.detail:
1. The word describes a person who is very concerned about observing the rites and visible practices of religion: the recited prayers, the offered sacrifices, the respected holy days. It is someone who wants their piety to be noticed and who focuses on form more than spirit. In James 1:26, the apostle warns one who "thinks he is religious" but lets his tongue wander: his external religion becomes vain because it does not produce true obedience of the heart.

2. This word emphasizes the aspect of external zeal for religious practices, without guaranteeing that the heart is transformed. A man can perform all the expected gestures — fasting, praying in public, making offerings — and yet deceive his own heart. That is why James insists: true religion begins with controlling the tongue and loving one's neighbor, not with the spectacle of piety.
G2357.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to respect" or "to honor" the rites of worship. It belongs to the family of words related to "religion" or "worship" (threskeia), which designate the set of religious practices. The etymology points to the idea of carefully submitting to the external forms of divine devotion, observing them rigorously.
G2357.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 1:26. The apostle uses it critically: he describes someone who imagines themselves to be "religious" — who sincerely believes they are observing true piety — but who in reality deceives themselves. The context shows that authentic religion is not just about observing external rites, but living in accordance with faith: controlling one's tongue, visiting orphans and widows, remaining unstained by the world (James 1:26-27). This word thus represents a superficial or deceptive form of piety.
G2357.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to ask an honest question: does my relationship with God rest on appearances or on a real transformation of the heart? The Bible rejects facade piety that consists of putting on a good face in public without private life and relationships reflecting that reality. True religion, according to James, is measured by our acts of mercy and our self-control, not by the number of our religious practices.

sens: To achieve a resounding victory, to prevail
To be led in triumph, to be the subject of a victory procession
To make someone or something triumph, to publicly highlight it
To defeat an enemy and subject them to public shame
G2358.detail:
1. To triumph means to achieve a decisive victory: God makes us "triumph in Christ" (2 Corinthians 2:14), which means that through faith in Christ, we are victorious in the spiritual battle and can proclaim God's victory everywhere.
2. The word originally evokes the Roman triumphal procession, where a victorious general was escorted by his troops and prisoners: the image of a victory publicly celebrated and visible to all.
3. To triumph over something also means to subject it to public shame: at Golgotha, Christ "disarmed the rulers and authorities, and made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross" (Colossians 2:15), meaning that through the cross, Jesus defeated the powers of evil and exposed them as defeated before all.
G2358.origine: The Greek word comes from θρίαμβος (thriambos), which designates both a festive hymn in honor of Bacchus and the Roman triumphal procession (triumphus in Latin), where the victorious general was publicly carried before the city to celebrate his victory. The biblical word takes up this image: it is less about a simple internal triumph than about a manifested victory, made visible and recognized by all.
G2358.emploi: The verb "to triumph" appears only twice in the New Testament, in two key passages of Paul. In 2 Corinthians 2:14, Paul asserts that God "always leads us in triumph in Christ": he speaks of a continuous and universal victory of Christ through which the believer participates in Jesus' dominion. In Colossians 2:15, Paul describes how Jesus personally "triumphed" over evil spiritual powers by his cross: the meaning is that of a resounding and public victory over the enemy, made manifest. In both cases, the word carries the charge of the Roman triumphal image: a total, public victory meant to be seen.
G2358.portee: This word invites the believer to understand their Christian life as a sharing in the victory of Christ. Not only did Jesus defeat sin, death, and the powers of evil at the cross, but this victory is manifested in the life of the Christian: we triumph with Him and for Him. This victory is not hidden or merely internal; it must shine through our testimony and our walk of faith. It is a call to live in the certainty that Christ reigns and that in Him we are already victors.

sens: Hair or fur on the head of a man
Fiber or hair from the body of animals
Tiny detail, insignificant thing
G2359.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to human hair, the fiber that grows on the head. John the Baptist wore clothing made of camel's hair (Matthew 3:4), while the sinful woman wiped Jesus' feet with her hair (Luke 7:38): the word speaks of what we see and touch every day.
2. It also applies to animal fur — the camel and the creatures of Revelation (Revelation 9:8) — it is the same physical reality, simply on another body.
3. Figuratively, hair represents extreme smallness, the insignificant. Jesus says that the hairs of our head are all counted (Matthew 10:30), and Paul promises that not a hair will be lost (Acts 27:34): this indicates that God knows and protects even the smallest details of our lives.
G2359.origine: The Greek word thrix comes from an ancient root that designates what grows, what is twisted or spun. In classical Greek, it is used for head hair and hair in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew word "sear" (שׂעַר), which has the same concrete meaning: hair, fur. It is a simple and direct word, without scholarly nuance.
G2359.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament. The Gospels mainly refer to the woman who anointed Jesus: she does so with her hair (Luke 7:38, John 11:2, John 12:3). Matthew and Luke report Jesus' teaching on counted hairs (Matthew 10:30, Luke 12:7), then Luke renews it for Jesus himself (Luke 21:18). Peter mentions the adornment of hair (1 Peter 3:3). Revelation describes creatures with hair like that of women (Revelation 9:8) and Christ with white hair (Revelation 1:14). Acts 27:34 promises that not a hair will be lost. The word remains literal: it never abstracts, but it carries a spiritual weight each time — tenderness, divine protection, or final judgment.
G2359.portee: This small word reveals God's infinite attention to His children. When Jesus says that our hairs are counted, He is not joking: it means that our Father sees and cares for every detail of our existence, even the humblest, even what seems insignificant in the eyes of the world. It is a comfort for the anxious heart: you are never forgotten, never neglected.

sens: To be seized with sudden fear or anxiety, to be alarmed
To be thrown into disarray, to lose one's calm or certainty
G2360.detail:
1. The verb describes the state of one who is struck by alarming news or a frightening noise: the soul or spirit is shaken, as if by an emotional shock. Jesus warns His disciples: "When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be troubled" (Mark 13:7). It is an inner agitation in the face of fear of tomorrow.
2. The word expands to denote losing one's footing, being shaken in one's trust or assurance. Paul writes to the Thessalonians not to be "troubled" by false claims that the day of the Lord has already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2): it is a disturbance of judgment, a mental confusion in the face of false doctrine.
G2360.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek "thrōos" which means noise or tumult. This root evokes the image of a noisy agitation, a disorder that disturbs the established order. The verb in the passive voice (which is the form used in the New Testament) means to be affected by this noise, this commotion. The central idea is that of a disturbance, a rupture of inner or outer peace.
G2360.emploi: The verb "trouble" appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the passive voice, in contexts where Jesus or Paul warns believers against a reaction of fear or confusion. In the two parallel passages of Matthew 24:6 and Mark 13:7, Jesus calls His disciples to remain calm in the face of rumors of war that will herald the end times: anxiety would only be a symptom of weak faith. In 2 Thessalonians 2:2, the apostle uses the same verb to urge his readers not to be shaken by false teachings about the timing of Christ's return. In all cases, the word denotes an emotional or intellectual disturbance that the believer must overcome through trust.
G2360.portee: This word speaks to every Christian confronted with fear, uncertainty, or the seduction of false doctrines. It reminds us that faith is not naivety, but a stable anchor in God: in the face of the world's crises or theological errors, the believer can remain calm, not because the problems are not real, but because God's promise remains. It is a call to self-control and spiritual vigilance.

sens: Small thick and compact mass
Drop or clot of thickened blood
G2361.detail:
1. A clot is a small solid, dense, and compact mass, contrasting with a smooth liquid. The image comes from the Greek verb "to thicken": something that has thickened, solidified, condensed.
2. In its only biblical usage, in Luke 22:44, this word describes Jesus' sweat in agony at Gethsemane: it becomes so thick that it coagulates, forming clots of blood that fall to the ground. The word emphasizes the extreme intensity of suffering — not ordinary sweat, but sweat that thickens to resemble congealed blood.
G2361.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to thicken" or "to condense." It describes what thickens, what passes from a liquid state to a pasty or solid state. The word is rare in Greek texts: the Bible uses it only once, which gives all its weight to this image of extreme agony.
G2361.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:44, during Jesus' prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane. Luke is the only one to report this detail of sweat becoming like congealed blood. It is a medical detail that highlights the physical intensity of the Lord's distress in the face of His impending passion. This unique mention gives it particular importance: it shows how deep and real Jesus' struggle was.
G2361.portee: For the believer, this detail reveals that Jesus truly suffered in body and soul before going to the cross. It was not a passive acceptance or without struggle, but a fight so intense that it marks the body itself. This honors the reality of His passion and reminds us of the price of our redemption.

sens: Seat of authority, furniture intended for a king or a high-ranking individual
Sovereign authority, royal or divine power
Dwelling or seat of God in heaven
Dignity and authority exercised by a reign or government
Celestial region from which God governs the universe
G2362.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the throne is the royal seat, the majestic furniture on which a king or sovereign sits to exercise his authority. It is a concrete, visible object, a symbol of power: we see it in Revelation 4:2, where John contemplates "him who was seated on the throne." 

2. The word also refers to the royal authority itself, the power to reign. In Luke 1:32, the angel announces concerning Jesus: "The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David" — it is not a piece of furniture that is given, but the right and power to reign.

3. By extension, the throne signifies heaven or God's heavenly dwelling, his place of residence and governance. Matthew 5:34 speaks of the "throne of God" to designate heaven itself, the seat from which God reigns over all things.

4. The term can also represent a function or a charge of government: in Matthew 19:28, Jesus promises the Apostles that they will sit "on twelve thrones," meaning they will exercise a judgment authority.

5. In heaven, the throne is the center from which all power and worship emanate. Revelation presents the throne of God surrounded by angels, elders, and living beings who worship him (Revelation 7:11): it is the seat of glory and absolute sovereignty.
G2362.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to place" or "to sit." In the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "kisseh," which designates the royal seat, the furniture on which the king sits to judge and govern. The throne was a visible symbol of power, ornate and elevated, from which the king spoke and rendered justice. The term has retained this dual dimension: both a material object and a symbol of sovereign power.
G2362.emploi: The word "throne" appears about 52 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Revelation (over 40 occurrences) and in Acts. It is used literally for royal seats (Matthew 25:31, where the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne), but very often in a figurative and theological sense. It designates heaven as God's seat (Acts 7:49), the authority conferred to the resurrected and glorified Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:8), the power granted to the Apostles (Luke 22:30), and even the authority of Satan or the beast (Revelation 2:13, Revelation 16:10). In John's visions, the throne of God is the cosmic center from which worship and creation flow: it radiates light, surrounded by celestial creatures proclaiming God's holiness and power. This vocabulary expresses that God reigns actively, visibly, sovereignly over heaven and earth.
G2362.portee: For the believer, contemplating the throne of God changes the perspective on reality. It means that God is not distant or absent: he actively reigns, governs history, and sees everything that happens. It also brings comfort in times of trouble: Hebrews 4:16 invites the believer to approach "with confidence to the throne of grace" to obtain mercy. Finally, knowing that Jesus is seated at the right hand of the Father, on the throne (Revelation 3:21), affirms his victory and eternal dignity, and promises the believer that he will also reign with him.

sens: City of Lydia (Asia Minor)
Major center of commerce for dyed fabrics
Seat of a first-century Church addressed in Revelation
G2363.detail:
1. Thyatira is a city located in Lydia, in Asia Minor (the region corresponding to present-day Turkey). It was an important center for trade and textile manufacturing, particularly for dyed fabrics, as evidenced by the mention of Lydia, a seller of purple from this city (Acts 16:14).
2. The city was prosperous due to its textile artisans. Lydia, who came from Thyatira and sold purple, became one of Paul's first converts in Europe (Acts 16:14), showing that this city was a thriving economic hub.
3. In John's time, Thyatira was one of the seven Churches of Asia to which Revelation addresses messages (Revelation 1:11; 2:18). The Church of Thyatira receives the longest message after that of Laodicea, indicating its ecclesiastical importance.
G2363.origine: The name Thyatira comes from the Greek Θυάτειρα. Thyatira was an ancient Greek city, traditionally founded by Lydian warriors. Its Greek name reflects its history and significance in the Hellenistic world during the Roman imperial period.
G2363.emploi: Thyatira appears four times in the New Testament, all in the books of Luke and Revelation. It is first mentioned in Acts 16:14, where Lydia, a God-fearing woman and seller of purple from Thyatira, becomes Paul's first convert in Philippi. In Revelation, Thyatira is listed among the seven Churches of Asia: it is named in 1:11 when John enumerates the seven Churches, and then it receives a detailed message from the Son of God in 2:18-24. This message praises the love, faith, service, and perseverance of the Church, but reprimands it for tolerating a woman who claims to be a prophetess and teaches erroneous doctrines (Revelation 2:18-24). The context suggests that it is a prosperous Church but facing internal doctrinal challenges.
G2363.portee: Thyatira reminds the reader that the Gospel took root in the prosperous urban centers of Asia Minor, reaching both merchants and artisans. The Church of Thyatira, despite its faithfulness and works, illustrates how a local Christian community can grow spiritually while needing to remain vigilant against false doctrines. Its example invites consideration of how faith is expressed concretely in a life of work and commerce, while remaining committed to the truth.

sens: Female child in relation to her parents
Term of affection or kind address towards a woman or young girl
Descendant, person from a lineage or group
City or region personified as a woman
G2364.detail:
1. Female child: this is the simplest and most common meaning. A father or mother refers to their female child with this word. In Matthew 9:18, a leader comes to ask Jesus to heal his dead daughter; in Mark 5:35, the father learns that his daughter has died.

2. Term of affection or address: Jesus uses this word to speak tenderly to a woman or young girl whom he heals. In Mark 5:34, he says to the woman with the issue of blood: "Daughter, your faith has healed you"; in Luke 8:48, the same words of comfort and healing.

3. Descendant or member of a lineage: the word designates someone who descends from an ancestor or belongs to a people. In Luke 1:5, Elizabeth is called "daughter of Aaron" (she descends from his priestly lineage); in Luke 13:16, the bent-over woman is called "daughter of Abraham" (she belongs to the people of Abraham).

4. City or region personified: a city is sometimes referred to as a "daughter," a poetic image that brings it to life. In Luke 23:28, Jesus speaks to the "Daughters of Jerusalem"; in Matthew 21:5, there is mention of the "daughter of Zion" (Zion itself, Jerusalem).
G2364.origine: The word comes from a very ancient Indo-European root that expresses the notion of birth and lineage. In Hebrew, we find בַּת (bat), which literally means "she who is born" or "descendant of." The Greek θυγάτηρ is the regular word used to translate this Hebrew term in the Greek Old Testament. The family of the word includes terms designating fatherhood and motherhood, as "daughter" implies a genetic and familial connection.
G2364.emploi: The word "daughter" appears 27 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and a few times in Acts and the epistles. It is first used in the literal sense: a female child in a family (Matthew 9:18, Mark 5:35, Luke 8:42). It also serves as a term of tender and kind address, especially when Jesus heals or comforts a woman (Mark 5:34, Luke 8:48). The word then designates belonging to a lineage or people: "daughter of Aaron" (Luke 1:5), "daughter of Abraham" (Luke 13:16). Finally, it is used poetically to personify a city or region, such as "Daughters of Jerusalem" (Luke 23:28) or "daughter of Zion" (Matthew 21:5, citing the Old Testament). In each context, the word expresses an intimate relationship and often a position of tenderness or kindness.
G2364.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus sees each person with affection and closeness, even the most suffering or excluded. By calling her "my daughter," he restores her human dignity and place. Understanding that this term also designates belonging to a people or lineage shows us that our Christian identity connects us to the great family of God, heirs of a promise that goes back to Abraham. The personification of cities as "daughters" invites us to view our relationship with the world with tenderness, not harshness.

sens: young girl, female child
term of affection or tenderness towards a little girl
G2365.detail: 1. The word designates a young girl, a female child. It is the affectionate diminutive of the Greek word for "daughter." In Mark 5:23, the father of this child pleads with Jesus saying: "My little girl is at the point of death" — she is dying, and he insists with the emotion of one who deeply loves his child. 2. It is a term of tenderness and affection. The Greek diminutive expresses here the love of the parent for their child, their vulnerability, the urgency of the heart surrounding them. In Mark 7:25, a mother whose little girl was possessed by an unclean spirit comes and falls at Jesus' feet, driven by that same maternal tenderness and desire to save her beloved child.
G2365.origine: The word comes from the classical Greek thugatèr ("daughter"). The suffix -ion adds a nuance of diminutiveness and affection, as when one says in French "fillette" or "little girl" instead of simply "daughter." This formation of the diminutive was common in late Greek to express tenderness. It is an ordinary word in the Greek family, reflecting how parents speak of their children with warmth.
G2365.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Gospel of Mark, in two accounts where Jesus heals a sick child. In Mark 5:23, it is Jairus, a synagogue leader, who pleads with Jesus for his little girl who is dying; Jesus raises her from the dead. In Mark 7:25, it is a foreign woman (a Phoenician) who implores Jesus for her daughter to be delivered from a demon. In both cases, the word carries the emotional weight of parental distress and the trust placed in Jesus to save the child. The diminutive reinforces the sense of urgency and the vulnerability of the child.
G2365.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus cares for the smallest, the children, those who can do nothing for themselves. The two mothers and the father who come to seek Jesus for their daughter show how faith consists of bringing to Jesus, without fear or calculation, the person we love the most. For us, this invites us to see in Jesus the one who can truly transform distress into salvation, and to entrust without reservation what is most precious to us.

sens: Violent atmospheric disturbance, whirlwind of wind and rain
Chaotic outcome, sudden crisis
G2366.detail:
1. The word θύελλα designates a violent meteorological phenomenon: a storm, a whirlwind, or a cyclone that blows with force and creates turbulent confusion. It is an extreme disturbance of the air, often associated with impressive and destructive phenomena. In Hebrews 12:18, the author describes the theophany at Sinai by listing what made the moment terrifying: among the terrifying divine manifestations are the burning mountain, clouds, darkness, and this storm — the chaotic atmosphere and unleashed forces surrounding the revelation of God.
2. By extension, the word can evoke any situation of crisis or sudden confusion, an event that shakes and disorganizes. Although the Greek word is used very literally in the New Testament, the image of the storm symbolizes moments when order collapses and uncertainty reigns.
G2366.origine: The word θύελλα comes from the verb θύω which means "to blow," "to make noise." The Aramaic Hebrew עֲרָפֶל (arafel) — darkness, mist, chaotic obscurity — is the term it often translates in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint). The storm is thus linked to the idea of violent movement and confusion: it is the chaos of unleashed air, darkness and noise together.
G2366.emploi: The word appears only once in use in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:18. It is found in a passage where the author contrasts the revelation of the Old Covenant at Sinai with that of the New Covenant in Christ. Hebrews 12:18 lists the terrors that accompanied God's presence at the mountain: the storm is presented as one of the frightening manifestations of the divine, alongside fire, cloud, and darkness. This choice of vocabulary reinforces the impression of a destructive and fearsome theophany, although this revelation is that of the Law, which the passage distinguishes from grace in Christ.
G2366.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the difference between the terrifying revelation of God under the Law and the approach in grace offered by Christ. The storm at Sinai reminds us that God's judgment and absolute holiness are real and fearsome — a storm of divine power that no creature can face without fear. For the Christian, this sheds light on the wonder of being able to approach God through Jesus without being annihilated: the divine storm has been calmed by Christ's sacrifice.

sens: Wood from a very fragrant African tree with ornamental veins
Luxury item and precious trade commodity in antiquity
G2367.detail:
1. θύϊνος refers to wood that comes from a specific African tree, the thuja, sought after for its intense fragrance and decorative colored veins. This wood was crafted to make furniture, boxes, and prestigious items.
2. In Revelation 18:12, scentwood appears among the precious goods that the merchants of the earth mourned over as they disappeared with the fall of Babylon: gold, silver, precious stones, purple, silk, and ivory. It was a luxury good reserved for the rich and kings, symbolizing wealth and earthly comfort.
G2367.origine: The Greek word θύϊνος comes from θυία or θύα, the name of the African tree from which this precious wood was obtained. The ancients also referred to this wood as "citrinus" in Latin. In the Greek Old Testament, this term sometimes corresponds to the Hebrew almougim, another exotic and rare wood.
G2367.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:12. John mentions it in his vision of the fall of great Babylon, listing the luxurious cargo of merchant ships. This unique usage reveals how John uses concrete and recognizable objects to evoke material wealth and the vanity of a world distant from God.
G2367.portee: This precious wood, listed among the earthly goods destined to disappear, invites the believer to distinguish between fleeting wealth and true riches. By enumerating these treasures that the merchants mourn, Revelation teaches us that possessions which seem inexhaustible and permanent are, in reality, fragile and perishable before God.

sens: fragrant substance burned in worship
precious offering in the temple
image of prayers ascending to God
luxury commercial item
G2368.detail:
1. Incense is a precious substance that is burned to produce fragrant smoke. In the Jewish temple, it is a regular offering: at the hour of incense (Luke 1:10), when Zechariah enters to offer it on the altar of incense (Luke 1:11), all the people pray outside, as this moment of worship is solemn and anticipated.
2. In John's vision (Revelation 5:8), incense becomes a symbol of the prayers of the saints: the elders hold bowls filled with incense, which are the prayers. Likewise (Revelation 8:3-4), the angel pours the incense on the golden altar before the throne of God, and the smoke rises with the prayers, showing that prayer ascends to God like a precious offering.
3. Incense also figures among the commercial riches of Babylon (Revelation 18:13), alongside spices and myrrh, indicating its high value in the ancient world.
G2368.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "to burn incense" (thumiáô). In Hebrew, the translated word is primarily "qetôret" (incense), which refers to the offering of incense burned twice daily on the golden altar of the sanctuary. Incense is inseparable from the biblical image of worship: the fire that burns, the smoke that rises, and the fragrance that pleases God.
G2368.emploi: The word appears six times in Greek, all in the New Testament. Three times in Luke (1:10, 1:11), it refers to the specific liturgical moment in the Jerusalem temple: the hour when incense is burned on the altar. Three times in Revelation, the meaning becomes spiritual and symbolic: incense represents the prayers of the saints ascending to God (5:8; 8:3-4), transforming the material rite into an image of communion between man and God. A final occurrence (18:13) brings it back to its concrete meaning as a precious good in commerce.
G2368.portee: This word invites the reader to see their prayers as a precious offering ascending to God, no less real than the visible smoke of incense. It also reminds us that worship is never a trivial matter: every moment, every gesture, every word addressed to God carries weight and dignity. The rare and costly incense tells us that our prayers are worthy of being offered to the King of kings.

sens: Portable container for burning incense
Fixed altar where incense is burned in the sanctuary
G2369.detail: 1. In its primary sense, the word refers to a small container, a censer that can be held in hand or transported. It is a vessel designed to hold the coals and incense to burn them together, as seen in the practices of ancient peoples. 2. In the context of Israelite worship, it refers to the golden altar specifically reserved for incense, located before the veil of the sanctuary: it is the altar of incense, distinct from the bronze altar of burnt offerings. In Hebrews 9:4, the text recalls that this sacred piece was part of the most holy objects of the tabernacle, along with the ark of the covenant and the vessel containing the manna.
G2369.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to burn incense" (thumiaoô), itself formed from the root of "incense" or "fragrant vapor" (thumiama). The starting image is that of vapor rising: the incense burned sends up a fragrant smoke to heaven, symbolizing prayer ascending to God. In Hebrew, this altar is called "altar of incense" (mizbeaḥ qeṭoret), and in Greek, the Old Testament generally translates it with this same word.
G2369.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:4, where the author describes the contents of the Holy of Holies of the tabernacle. In this passage, "the golden altar for incense" is presented as one of the three essential pieces of furniture in this very holy place, along with the ark of the covenant and the golden vessel containing the manna. This context shows that the word here refers to the fixed altar of the sanctuary, a major symbol of Judeo-Israelite worship and of communion between God and His people through prayer embodied in the ascending incense.
G2369.portee: The altar of incense reminds Christians that prayer ascends to God as a precious offering. In ancient worship, this altar was placed at the heart of the sanctuary, near the throne of God represented by the ark: it is a living image that our prayers and adorations reach the Lord. This altar invites us to understand that our prayer is not in vain, but is received by God as a pleasing fragrance.

sens: To burn incense in religious service
To offer incense to God as an act of worship
To perform an act of veneration through the smoke of incense
G2370.detail:
1. The verb refers to the action of burning incense, that is, to consume aromatic perfumes on an altar or brazier so that they produce fragrant smoke. The incense rising to heaven was an essential element of temple worship, a concrete symbol of prayer and adoration ascending to God.

2. In the biblical religious context, burning incense was a priestly privilege reserved for the priests. The Segond translates it as "offering the incense" in Luke 1:9, where Zechariah, dressed in his priestly duties, enters the inner sanctuary of the temple to perform this service. It is an act of great solemnity: only the priest designated by lot could do this each day.

3. Spiritually, this act represents the offering of prayer and the worship of the people rising before God. The burning incense becomes the image of intercession and pleasing worship, a tangible way of saying: "I offer myself, my prayers rise to you, Lord."
G2370.origine: The Greek verb θυμιάω comes from θύω (thúō, "to sacrifice"), an ancient verb related to the idea of offering a sacrifice. However, it is specialized by the context: it specifically refers to the act of burning fragrant incense, which transforms a terrestrial material into an invisible offering rising to heaven. In biblical Hebrew, the equivalent word is קָטַר (qâṭar, "to make smoke burn"), which appears mainly in descriptions of temple worship. The Greek of the Septuagint uses θυμιάω to translate this Hebrew term when the Old Testament speaks of the incense of the sanctuary.
G2370.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:9. It is at the moment when the angel Gabriel appears to Zechariah. Zechariah, a priest of the division of Abijah, is chosen by lot — a distinguished honor — to enter the temple and burn the incense of worship. This ordinary act, repeated daily in the temple, becomes extraordinary: it is during this service that Zechariah receives the announcement of the birth of John the Baptist. The use of the verb emphasizes the solemnity and holiness of the moment: God intervenes at the very heart of Levitical worship.
G2370.portee: This word reminds the believer that prayer and worship rise before God as a precious offering. The image of the burning incense rising helps to understand how our intercession and worship are pleasing to God and received by Him. It is also an invitation to see in the ordinary service of worship an act of great dignity: it is by serving faithfully that we encounter God and receive His promises.

sens: To be furious and in conflict with someone
To harbor passionate hostility against someone
G2371.detail:
1. The word describes a state of intense anger mixed with conflict: it is not a simple cold dispute, but a confrontation where passion and emotion dominate.
